articles.title: 'Slow Horses' to Hit 10-Season Milestone With Apple TV Renewal
articles.content: Apple has renewed its popular British spy drama "Slow Horses" for ninth and tenth seasons, extending its considerable lead as Apple TV 's longest-running original series by season, according to Deadline . Six seasons of Slow Horses have already been released, with seasons seven and eight already confirmed before the latest renewal. The order for seasons nine and ten extends its lead as the ‌Apple TV‌ original with the most seasons commissioned. The commitment puts "Slow Horses" well ahead of other established Apple originals. "For All Mankind," which debuted when the service launched in 2019, will finish with season six . "Slow Horses" has also maintained an exceptional critical reception, with all six seasons holding critics' scores of 95% or higher on Rotten Tomatoes . Seasons two and four have perfect 100% ratings, while the latest season holds 98%. The news answers recent uncertainty about the show's future. Cast member Olivia Cooke had suggested just days earlier that season eight could mark its conclusion. The television series is catching up with the book series it is based on that began 16 years ago. Author Mick Herron has published nine main "Slough House" novels since the first one debuted in 2010, with gaps of between one and three years between installments. The latest, "Clown Town," arrived in 2025, three years after "Bad Actors." Those two books provide the material for seasons seven and eight, raising the possibility that seasons nine and ten could move beyond the published novels. Apple has not confirmed that direction, with a spokesperson telling Deadline that story details for the additional seasons would follow. Produced by See-Saw Films, "Slow Horses" centers on an outpost of MI5 where agents are sent after damaging their professional reputations. Gary Oldman plays their boss, "Jackson Lamb," alongside a cast that includes Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Jonathan Pryce, and Cooke. The first six seasons are available to stream now on ‌Apple TV‌. articles.title: Microsoft is hiking cloud prices in India — but dropping costs in China and other markets
articles.content: Microsoft raising cloud prices for customers in India, New Zealand by 15%, 10% Currency fluctuations have afforded three countries to get cheaper cloud prices Brazil changes also on the cards, Japan announcement expected later Microsoft has confirmed the details of its latest currency adjustments in a bid to keep local pricing more closely aligned with its global pricing levels and to account for exchange rate fluctuations, and it's bad news for India which is set to see cloud pricing increases of 15.7%. New Zealand will also see a 10% rise, while the two nations will also see rises of up to 20% and 10% across on-prem pricing. But not all countries are seeing price hikes – China (-8.5%), Norway (-5.9%) and Australia (-4%) will each see a decrease in cloud pricing in line with currency exchange rates. These three countries see no change to on-prem pricing. Microsoft announces its latest exchange rate-linked pricing adjustments It's worth noting that individual products may see slightly different adjustments based on rounding rules and also how the prices are calculated, but the above percentages offer a preview into the sort of changes customers in these five nations can expect to see in the new year. The company confirmed in a blog post that the changes will come into effect from January 1, 2027, as part of a new scheme it introduced in July 2026 whereby the hyperscaler would adjust prices each January for greater predictability, rather than at random points throughout the year. Microsoft is also looking to adjust its Brazil pricing following the implementation of the nation's tax reform, while Japan will remain on its previous annual April cadence (with an announcement on track for February 2027). It's argues that the revisions will help maintain competitive and regionally consistent prices for its cloud services, but some customers worry that currency fluctuations can make identical services more expensive or cheaper depending on where customers are billed. Crucially though, these adjustments are purely a response to global currency fluctuations, and it's not a sign that Microsoft is raising its prices across the board.
articles.author: Craig Hale

articles.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
articles.content: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from Washington, DC, to San Francisco, and accommodation so Ars could try its new driver assistance systems. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year , the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive . Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel. While most automakers want a reputation associated with safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, then a decade later started adding active safety systems like antilock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes, and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineerspeak. “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines. articles.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
articles.content: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain,…

articles.title: Google: AI agent turned a security patch into a working exploit with no human help
articles.content: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report . This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN , CyberStrikeAI , HexStrike AI , and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®

articles.title: Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric
articles.content: Celestial AI’s dream of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at a distance will soon be a reality as part of a new collaboration between Marvell Technology and system integrator Penguin Solutions to build a photonic memory fabric. Marvell acquired the underlying technology for the fabric from Celestial AI for $3.5 billion in February. It comprises a memory expansion module with two stacks of HBM3e totaling 72 GB along with support for eight channels of DDR5 stacked atop a silicon photonic interposer with 7.2 Tbps (900 GB/s) of bidirectional bandwidth. “What we provide in this appliance is what we call a Photonic Fabric memory module… We provide these modules to Penguin, and they build the box, do all the power management, do the software, and all the management layer,” Preet Virk, senior VP of Marvell’s photonic fabric biz, tells El Reg. Penguin’s first appliances based on the tech will support 16 of these memory modules for up to 16 TB of DDR5 and 1 TB of HBM, with future systems capable of scaling to twice the DDR5 capacity. With 57.6 Tbps of bandwidth distributed via a Marvell-designed optical fiber shuffle, each appliance supports up to 16 servers either via a network interface card, or via co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged optical (NPO) modules. If you’re not familiar, CPO modules are typically integrated directly into the compute or switch ASIC, while NPO modules are a sort of half measure. They connect electrically to the host, whether that’s a CPU, GPU, or some other ASIC, and the rest of the fabric optically. NPO is expected to play a major role in the next generation of rack-scale systems from Nvidia and AMD, as it provides better serviceability and lower blast radius than baking photonic chiplets directly into CPUs or GPUs. Through a software layer, which we’re told was developed by Penguin, each system can access the entire shared memory space, similar to how systems connecting to network-attached storage would have access to the appliance's full capacity. As we understand it, a lot of this functionality is made possible today through CXL 3.1 compatible NICs and host CPUs, like AMD’s shiny new Venice CPUs. However, for NPO- and CPO-based memory, Virk tells us that CXL can be bypassed entirely. The implications of this tech should be obvious. If memory can be shared and pooled across multiple servers, each of those servers doesn't need as much of its own DRAM, possibly saving some money. In addition to facilitating communications, Virk says, the software also allows for several memory tiering modes by which customers can expose the resources to connected systems. For the most part, these follow typical CXL memory tiering conventions, with the exception of an HBM cache-through mode that Virk says will enable users to extract the performance of HBM with the capacity of DDR5. This mode essentially treats the HBM as a read/write cache. Frequently accessed files are written to and read from HBM first before being pushed into standard DDR5 as they get stale. Marvell and Penguin are positioning the new memory appliance as an alternative to storage-based key value (KV) cache offload. AI inference generates large KV caches, which are used to track model state across chat sessions, and long-running agents. Depending on the context length, these caches can be both computationally expensive to recompute and large to keep in memory. Because of this, inactive KV caches are often offloaded to DRAM or flash memory, since it’s faster to store and copy them than to recompute them if and when a session is restored. Marvell contends that by offloading KV caches from HBM directly to these memory appliances, customers can achieve better performance and higher memory utilization. Beyond AI-adjacent workloads, this technology also has potential to reduce the amount of DRAM required for individual systems, a concept we explored in greater depth earlier this year, and one that Meta has already embraced in its own datacenters. articles.title: Nike Vaporfly 5 first look: 5 big upgrades coming to Nike’s iconic carbon racing shoe
articles.content: I vividly remember the launch of the Nike Vaporfly 4% in 2017 — the bright blue shoe with a carbon plate that promised to help runners get 4% faster on race day. It changed how we think about race-day shoes for good. To celebrate the shoe’s 10th anniversary, Nike has announced the Vaporfly 5, the lightest, most aggressive version of the Vaporfly to date. Let’s put aside how old this all makes me feel and dive into the details of the redesigned racer. Vaporfly 5: What’s new? Nike has said this is its lightest, fastest, most aggressive Vaporfly yet. The shoe has a redesigned Wave Flyplate, which contours around the foot to improve stability and increase energy return. There’s a new midsole foam: ZoomX LT, which is 17% lighter and offers 8% more energy return than standard ZoomX. Plus, the shoe looks different from the Vaporfly we know and love, with a sizeable cutout on the side of the shoe to allow the Wave Flyplate to do its thing. Tom’s Guide was invited to see a sneak peek of the shoe, and here’s what we learned: Wave Flyplate: Unlike the traditional carbon plate we’ve come to expect from our racing shoes, the new Wave Flyplate is lower in the heel, then sprouts upward under the midfoot to sit under the arch. Nike says this creates a spring-like sensation under the arch, while the wider midfoot adds stability to the shoe. ZoomX LT : There are two different midsole foams in the shoe. Nike’s new ZoomX LT sits closest to your foot, offering more energy return. The ZoomX midsole foam we know and love sits underneath the plate for a bouncy, responsive underfoot experience. Reduced weight versus the Vaporfly 4: Nike has confirmed this shoe is lighter than the previous iteration of the shoe, with a Vapor mesh upper and the lighter ZoomX LT midsole foam. GOATEK rubber outsole: The thin outsole is designed to provide race-day grip in all weather conditions. What does it look like? You can see from inital images of the super shoe that theres a sizeable cutout on the side of the shoe. This is to allow the wave-shaped plate to perform as intended, and offer the spring sensation under the arch of the foot. When is it available, and how much will it cost? The shoe will cost $225, but it won’t be hitting the market until fall 2027, so we’ve got a while to wait. We will bring you our review once we’ve got the shoes on our feet, so stay tuned. articles.title: Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’
articles.content: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella is betting Copilot can do for AI at work what Windows did for the PC. (GeekWire File Photo / Todd Bishop) It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence. These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”). Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS .” Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance. Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead. Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions. The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes. Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks. Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer. The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform. Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well. Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps. The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works. If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf. “We increasingly…

articles.title: 'iPhone 20 Pro' Rumored to Be Based on iPhone Air
articles.content: Next year's "iPhone 20 Pro" models will use the same glass design as the iPhone Air , but with more pronounced curvature along all four sides, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ." In a new post on Weibo, the leaker said the device would use the same glass material as the ‌iPhone Air‌, adjusted to have greater curvature and produce a four-sided curved effect. The accompanying hashtag refers specifically to an "iPhone 20 Pro" with a four-sided curved, "all-glass" design. An illustration shared with the post depicts rounded front and rear glass meeting a narrow, polished, gold-colored metallic frame. Physical side buttons, antenna lines, and a protruding rear camera assembly remain visible. Taken together with earlier rumors and the post's accompanying illustration, the repeated comparisons suggest a design somewhere between the iPhone X and ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ provides a reference for the slim profile and a more modern iPhone design, while the more pronounced glass curvature recalls the rounded edges of the iPhone X. Both feature a polished frame. The latest claim builds on Fixed Focus Digital's previous report that Apple had modified ‌iPhone Air‌ manufacturing equipment to produce more rounded glass components for the 20th anniversary models. The leaker said the changes had helped reduce manufacturing costs, while substantially improving thinness and heat dissipation. In a still-earlier report , the same leaker also claimed that a supply chain facility had completed renovations ahead of "iPhone 20" production, with manufacturing quality expected to be roughly comparable to the first-generation ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back. The broader design picture aligns with Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman 's reporting that Apple's anniversary Pro models will feature glass that curves into the sides from both the front and rear, with a thin metal band between the two panels. Gurman has also described thinner display bezels and curved glass around all corners and edges, in what he expects to be the biggest overhaul of the Pro line since the iPhone X. Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 . While leakers have variably referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," Apple's naming plans remain unclear. It seems plausible that the company could skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to its introduction of the iPhone X in 2017. articles.title: The Jensen Huang saga could be the beginning of the end of the AI bubble – or just a boon for competitors
articles.content: KETTLE Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia after a trio of affairs that include an alleged Chinese spy and two of his subordinates, turning the week into one that's shaken the tech sector. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify , Apple Music, or YouTube . Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live. What will become of Nvidia now that its only leader in 33 years, and one whose vision shaped the company into one of the largest in the world, is gone? Who will take charge? Will other chipmakers take advantage of the chaos to surpass the Geforce maker? Will Jensen be the one to put a pin to the AI bubble? Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, systems editor Tobias Mann , and reporter Dan Robinson to talk about the Jensen Huang affair(s) and how the misdeeds of one of AI's biggest names could reshape the entire industry on this week's episode. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hey everyone and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg Reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and the big news on the tech industry's mind this week is the ouster of Nvidia founder, CEO, president, and board member Jensen Huang over allegations that he not only had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, but also at least two Nvidia employees who were his subordinates. Nvidia's been shaped into one of the most valuable companies in the world over the past thirty-three years, and Huang has played a pivotal, if not the pivotal, role in that ascension, meaning his controversial departure is going to rock the industry, if not the greater world. With me to discuss this is our systems editor Tobias Mann and Reg reporter Dan Robinson. Thanks to you both for coming on. Dan Robinson (00:42) Hi. Tobias Mann (00:43) Good to be here. Brandon (00:43) Quite the week, huh? It seems like we went from Jensen’s just going to survive this spy kerfuffle to the board basically seeming to demand his resignation in the course of a few days, right? So Dan, bring us up to speed on the timeline here, what happened? Dan Robinson (01:01) Well, it all happened over the last couple of weeks. That was when the story first surfaced, or it was first reported in the media, of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who happened to work for this company in Singapore that bought a lot of Nvidia's products. Brandon (01:30) Right, company was Megaspeed, right? And her name's Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, coincidence. Dan Robinson (01:36) So it's all happened fairly quickly, but like you say, at the start of this week, it all seemed like Jensen could weather the storm. We were discussing this in our editorial chat and we thought that basically there isn't really anybody who could replace him, or so we thought. He practically is Nvidia, and it's been his vision that's driven the company for so long. But then he came out and he confessed and said he was sorry to all the Nvidia employees. Then the second affair came to light and very quickly, on November 11th actually, Wednesday, he handed in his resignation and it was accepted by the board. So we got to hear about it yesterday [Thursday] when they announced it and it was filed with the SEC. Brandon (03:03) And since then a third affair has come out, right? The New York Times published a finding. Tobias Mann (03:06) Just a few hours later, yeah. Dan Robinson (03:08) It seems so. Makes you wonder how many others may be about to come out in the following days. Brandon (03:13) We're not going to speculate, but my gosh, it seems like that leather jacket really made him irresistible. It’s kind of crazy, right? It seems like the internal affairs with Nvidia employees are the ones that sort of broke the board's back, right? The spy affair seemed like it was kind of like…. Apparently American authorities have basically said they've found no direct evidence to say she is a spy.…
articles.author: Brandon Vigliarolo

articles.title: Amazon’s Starlink rival sees major setback after 40 satellites destroyed in rocket failure
articles.content: Amazon has suffered a major setback in its plans to offer a viable Starlink rival, after 40 satellites destined for low Earth orbit (LEO) were destroyed. Just ten minutes after the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 in Cape Canaveral, Florida, on Sunday, there was an “anomaly,” meaning that the rocket “failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” The language seems quite vague, but the United Launch Alliance (ULA) says that data needs to be analyzed “to understand what occurred today.” And LIFTOFF of the first Vulcan Amazon Leo mission, carrying 40 broadband satellites to low Earth orbit! https://t.co/dv1MSjJUMF November 15, 2026 Shortly after the triumphant takeoff clip was shared by the ULA, above, the space tech firm updated its X feed with a confirmation that its mission on behalf of Amazon failed. Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today. ULA exists to provide assured access to space for our nation and for the customers who depend on us. That purpose is why we take on some of the hardest missions in spaceflight, and why we hold ourselves to the standard of mission success. Today, we did not meet that standard.We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.ULA is committed to full transparency with our customers, and they will have visibility into the investigation process, which utilizes rigorous methodology and corrective action.We will provide further updates when new information becomes available. November 15, 2026 Sadly for Amazon, the ULA, and folks who want a viable substitute for Starlink in the satellite internet business, this failure will surely delay the full commercialization of this service. ISPReview notes that Amazon has successfully launched 392 Kuiper communications satellites, but needs at least 500 for basic global coverage. Moreover, Amazon Leo service’s transition from the current commercial beta phase to launching properly at the end of 2026 now looks uncertain. Reports indicate Amazon has already manufactured 1,000 satellites, but ULA, which is a joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin , will need to analyze and assure customers that Sunday’s failure won’t be repeated. ULA's Vulcan vehicle had already been out of action for nine months after technical investigations into issues with its solid rocket side boosters and core BE-4 engines (made by Amazon Blue Origin). For some context, the ULA has (or had) a great track record. Sunday's incident was its first total mission failure in its 20-year history. Early telemetry from the organization is already pointing towards some suspected causes of the destruction of the 40 satellites. Likely fault candidates include the first-stage BE-4 engines burning longer than planned, and there may have been some altitude issues near staging. The headline failure and essential careful analysis of the anomaly won’t hold up Amazon’s other launch partners, though. A week from today, the Amazon Leo constellation is set to grow by 36 more satellites. They will be sent into orbit aboard a European Ariane 64 Block 2 (LE-04) rocket. Amazon has approval for an initial constellation of 3,236 LEO broadband satellites, with 392 now in orbit, plus 5,105 for 5G service. Satellite tracking sites suggest Starlink already has 11,200+ satellites in orbit.

articles.title: 'Slow Horses' will continue with unexpected ninth and tenth season order
articles.content: Despite rumors of Apple TV hit "Slow Horses" coming to an end, industry sources report that it's been given two further seasons. Don't put your feet up just yet. The sixth season of spy thriller "Slow Horses" concluded on Apple TV in October 2026 with a teaser for the following season. But then star Olivia Cooke, who plays Sid Baker, said the show was to end with its eighth season. Specifically, she said that she was currently "shooting the last season," and that this was what she had been told. Plus she said that the case and crew were "melancholy, distracted," because of the impending end. However, Deadline magazine now reports that Apple has ordered two further seasons. That will bring the show up to ten, which is unprecedented for an Apple TV series. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: William Gallagher <wg@williamgallagher.com>

articles.title: One UI 9.5 may let you set a custom greeting for Call Screening
articles.content: TL;DR An early build of One UI 9.5 contains references to an upgraded version of Call Screening that would let users set custom greetings. Call Screening currently lets you change the voice or tweak the speech rate, but doesn’t let you type in a custom greeting. Samsung introduced Call Screening with the Galaxy S26 series earlier this year to answer incoming calls on the user’s behalf. Samsung introduced Call Screening with the Galaxy S26 series earlier this year, and One UI 9.5 could make it more customizable. Call Screening can answer incoming calls on your behalf and give you a text transcript of the conversation as it happens. While it lets you change the language, voice, or speech rate, you can’t modify the greeting message that callers hear. Samsung’s next One UI release may change that. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. Digging into an early One UI 9.5 build, we have uncovered a handful of strings that reference the ability to modify the opening message incoming callers hear with Call Screening enabled. While we couldn’t surface visuals of this Call Screening upgrade, code strings suggest users can type their own greeting.
articles.author: Chethan Rao

articles.title: Opinion: Moravec’s paradox explains why physical AI needs a sense of touch
articles.content: Ron Zukerman, innovation director at Vishay Precision Group When people first started trying to build human‑like robots, the roadmap seemed clear. The assumption was simple: if something feels hard for us, it must be hard for machines too. So, we treated things like playing chess, doing advanced math, or analysing legal arguments as the “real” […]

We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten. Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise. articles.content: Credit: Shimul Sood / Android Authority TL;DR A new leak claims Samsung could bring variable aperture cameras to the Galaxy S28 Pro and Galaxy S28 Ultra in 2028. The potential comeback follows Apple introducing a variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and similar interest from Chinese Android brands. Samsung is expected to skip the hardware on early 2027’s Galaxy S27 series due to added cost and device thickness. Samsung last shipped a mechanical variable aperture camera on the Galaxy S10 series in 2019, and rumors of a comeback have circulated since late last year , as Apple’s plans to ship a variable aperture camera on the iPhone became clearer. While earlier evidence suggested Samsung was testing the hardware again , later reports indicated the upcoming Galaxy S27 lineup would skip the upgrade because of added cost and thickness. Now, a new leak points to the Galaxy S28 series as the likely target for the feature’s return. According to leaker Yogesh Brar on X , variable aperture cameras could make a comeback on the Galaxy S28 Pro and Galaxy S28 Ultra.

articles.title: 'Every organization has to invest in getting this right': Proofpoint CEO warns the agentic AI age will mean a whole new generation of cyber threats
articles.content: The CEO of Proofpoint has urged companies of all sizes to be on guard against new and advanced cyber threats built and enabled by the rise of AI. Speaking at the company’s recent Proofpoint Protect Tour London 2026 event, Sumit Dhawan warned that customers should, “think of AI agents as insiders in your environment” as the number of AI-assisted attacks continues to rise. The company recently released research claiming AI enables cybercriminals to operate at a scale 'never seen before' - so how does it suggest companies stay safe? Defend and Access with Intent In his keynote, Dhawan declared that “the concept of time in cybersecurity keeps shrinking”, giving the example of a recent cyber heist which took place in just 27 seconds. “An agentic toolkit is now able to identify vulnerabilities, issue attacks, and create multiple social engineering campaigns in an automated fashion,” he added, “in this world, we believe that making sure that your human perimeter is protected, because reachability becomes one of the biggest things - and the defence needs to be done with proper understanding of intent.” Dhawan outlined Proofpoint’s strategy of Defend with Intent, and Access with Intent, the former looking to understand where attacks originate and how to build resiliency and defense, especially with AI giving attackers a whole new arsenal of tools. The latter looks to ensure humans and AI can continue to work effectively together, as agents don’t access data or apps the same way humans do, necessitating a whole new approach to make sure company systems are safe. "AI journey" In a later media Q&A session, Dhawan and Daniel Blackford, head of threat research at Proofpoint, expanded on the role that AI is playing in these new threats, noting how quickly the threat landscape has changed. “I think things have changed,” Blackford says, “threat actors have gone on a similar AI journey that a lot of us have,” although he notes that there is still an adoption and learning curve, as attackers and defenders alike try to discover the best way to utilize AI. “The problem I see is not whether it's hype or not - but what you do about it,” Dhawan adds, noting how the need for constant and rapid reaction to threats is quickly going to become fatiguing for workers - so the crucial consideration is what businesses do about it. “It's somewhat of a thankless job, you're always chasing a major threat,” he notes, “ (but) every organization has to invest in getting the right configuration of access and data.” “Defenders have had a window where we've been ahead of where threat actors were with using AI - but that window is shrinking,” adds Blackford. This may be particularly key for small businesses - and I ask Dhawan and Blackford what advice they have for SMBs looking to stay ahead of the latest threats. “For small businesses, in the past, cybersecurity for them was a little bit of basic hygiene - do I have my antivirus, my firewall, some kind of email spam filtering that also catches some of these threats - now, it’s a real issue,” Dhawan says, pointing to Proofpoint’s recent acquisition of Hornetsecurity as its bid to offer thorough protection for SMBs. “It’s quite important for small and medium businesses to take (cybersecurity) more seriously now than they ever have,” Blackford adds, noting that these firms could suffer immensely from a lack of reputation due to suffering an attack. (Image credit: iStock) Ultimately, Proofpoint sees its mission as attempting to protect its customers from the biggest number of threats it can - with its recent acquisition of Varonis demonstrating its intent to offer AI-related protection like never before. “Protection is not meaningful if it doesn't work with everything you have in your environment,” Dhawan noted, pointing out that as the average business can now see millions of AI prompts and actions in a typical year - a mammoth task which simply cannot be manually audited and investigated by humans alone. “We're doing…

articles.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
articles.content: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal…

articles.title: How many times are you paying to store the same file?
articles.content: Pick any busy project folder and count the copies. There's one on the file server, one in a cloud bucket and one on each laptop that needed it at a usable speed. If a team got fed up with sync and built its own workaround, there's another in there too. The storage bill pays for every one of them. The Register and LucidLink are hosting senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November to compare how they're bringing that number down. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. Request a place Nobody keeps duplicates for fun. They're what people do when files have to move between sites faster than sync allows. Every copy IT can't see into is a security question as well as a cost, so the duplicates you don't know about matter most. What the table wants to hear is how others got the copies down without ripping out storage they've already paid for, or the governance built around it. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, so people say what worked and what didn't. Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers. Nobody presents. Drinks are at 6.30pm and dinner around one table runs until 9pm. Places are limited. Request a place at the 24 November dinner Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally. Sponsored by LucidLink.

articles.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
articles.content: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators. NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation.” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained. Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems. A compute chameleon LANL is one of several labs tasked with ensuring that the US’ nuclear deterrent remains effective decades after underground testing was banned. The lab is also responsible for running simulations on energy sources like fuel candidates for future fusion reactors. Both of these workloads, Shipman tells us, fall into a category called multi-physics simulations. These workloads aren’t really one workload, but multiple simulations that can have wildly different compute requirements. A “good example is inertial confinement fusion. At the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, you're using lasers to implode a fuel capsule, and the goal is to generate more energy through yield than you do from depositing energy to the capsule,” Shipman explained. “That's inherently multiphysics.” There are simulations for the lasers, the hydrodynamics within the fuel capsule, and the chemistry and material interactions taking place during the fusion process. The problem, Shipman explains, is that a system that’s ideal for one of those simulations may not be well suited to others. “Identifying one specific platform that is optimal for that type of simulation is challenging.” CPUs, he says, are well suited to workloads with large serial sections, irregular access patterns, and jobs that benefit from deep cache hierarchies. Meanwhile, GPUs are fantastic for dense, matrix-multiplication heavy workloads. "Where NextSilicon fits in is being able to reconfigure to match the workload, on demand,” Shipman said. “The hope is that we won't have to make these rigid determinations upfront like, ‘we need this much CPU or we need this much GPU.’ We can use a much more adaptable, reconfigurable architecture to meet the workflow where it is at.” A closer look at Maverick 2 Despite some visual similarities to Nvidia’s current crop of GPUs, Maverick-2 is not a GPU. Instead it employs a dataflow architecture which overlaps communication and computation. Rather than waiting for load-store operations to shuffle data around as you would with a conventional CPU or GPU, the chips themselves comprise a grid of arithmetic logic units (ALUs) which are configured to perform an operation like addition or multiplication in the order that they’re needed. Data is computed as it moves from one ALU to the next, a bit like how a ball moves through a Rube Goldberg contraption. This can make dataflow architectures…

articles.title: Jailbroken PS4 runs 9-billion-parameter AI model at up to 43 tokens per second
articles.content: Developer Leonardo Alegría’s open-source project Garlic LLM lets a jailbroken PS4 run the 9-billion-parameter Qwen3.5-9B AI model offline on the console’s 2013-era GPU. The app talks to the GPU directly, and the model is shrunk to about 4.5GiB to fit in the console’s memory, running at 31 to 39 tokens per second. The project, named after the memory the GPU reads directly — its sibling memory type is “Onion” — relies on a PS4 running GoldHEN, which is a homebrew enabler for exploited consoles. Garlic LLM is a free, single 5.66GB download, available on Hugging Face and installable through the PS4’s Package Installer, with about 6GB free needed, or 12GB if the package is first copied to the console’s internal disk. The developer tested it on a base/Slim PS4 on firmware 11.52. (Image credit: Leonardo Alegría/Garlic LLM) It’s capable of voice conversation, with spoken replies in seven languages through the Chatterbox speech model and the chat model running at about 22 tokens per second. A held controller button also lets it take dictation with Nvidia’s Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 speech-to-text model, which supports 25 European languages. Parakeet models also power local transcription and dictation apps such as Meetily and Hex. The main model is Alibaba’s small open-weight Qwen3.5-9B, which, at the claimed 31 to 39 tokens per second in text chat — the prompt and test method are not given — is usable on the console. The closest comparison is the PS5LM fork , which runs llama.cpp as a native app on the PS5 and reaches the console’s AMD GPU through PS5_Vulkan, a port of the RADV driver. The open-source llama.cpp is a widely used program for running language models locally, and RADV is the open-source driver that lets AMD GPUs run Vulkan, the graphics and compute API. On the PS4 there is no such driver layer for homebrew; Garlic LLM uses neither llama.cpp nor a Vulkan port, or so it would appear. The model’s operations, such as matrix multiplies over 4-bit weights, are compute kernels written in OpenCL C and compiled with LLVM for AMD’s Graphics Core Next (GCN) architecture. The weights are kept in that “Garlic” memory, while the CPU side, in plain C, handles the tokenizer, the interface, text rendering, and audio. The pipeline runs from the prompt to the CPU tokenizer, then, for each token, a PM4 command buffer — the low-level commands a graphics driver would normally generate, which, in this case, the app builds itself — and the GCN kernels, before the token is displayed or spoken. The whole thing is built with the open-source OpenOrbis PS4 toolchain. One immediate question is how you fit a 9-billion-parameter model in the console’s 8GB of memory , which the CPU and GPU share. At 8 bits per weight, you have one byte per parameter, meaning you’d need at least 9GB, with typically more than that required overall. Part of the answer is 4-bit (“Q4”) weights, which take half as much, although 3-bit (“Q3”) weights, at about 3.5 bits with scales, are used for the two largest matrices in each layer. Using the combination gets you to about 4.5GiB, versus about 4.9GiB if it were all 4-bit. The attention, or KV, cache is also 4-bit, which lets a 16K-token context fit, in comparison to the model’s native 256K. The Parakeet dictation model adds 0.33GiB and the Chatterbox voice models 0.29GiB and 0.09GiB, for a grand total of 5.23GiB, or 5.62GB, which closely matches the 5.66GB package size. The next question is performance. Qwen3.5 comes with a multi-token prediction (MTP) head, and Garlic LLM uses it to draft up to two tokens ahead , with the full model verifying. This matches what the model was trained for, and the vLLM instructions on Alibaba’s model card use two speculative tokens. The project credits this for its chat speed on 2013 hardware. Code also comes out faster with this setup, at up to 43 tokens per second. Also detailed is the default temperature, or model variability, which is 0.7 — Alibaba recommends 0.7 for general tasks with thinking…

articles.title: Intel sued by shareholders for misleading investors after stock plunges 29%
articles.content: Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the company of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters . Go deeper with TH Premium: Chipmaking (Image credit: tsmc) Analyzing TSMC's fab expansion roadmap — multi-fab N2 ramp, CoWoS, SoIC, and uncorking bottlenecks Leading-edge foundry roadmaps for TSMC, Intel, and Samsung ASML's roadmap for chipmaking lithography tools examined Chinese chipmaking tool roadmaps examined The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities. "Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads. While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the company's stock price in October. Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the company's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026. A similar update could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010. Intel's shareholders also allege that the company had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity. Intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the company's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the company's shares between July 23 and October 29,…
articles.author: Anton Shilov

articles.title: Apple’s first smart glasses are finally taking shape — here are 3 big ways it will stand out
articles.content: The worst-kept secret in Cupertino is finally spilling out onto the timeline. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , Apple is targeting WWDC 2027 to launch its first pair of smart glasses . Back in 2025, I wrote that visionOS was quietly setting the stage for a killer pair of smart specs — completely sidestepping the bulky, overpriced Apple Vision Pro. Well, turns out that prediction was dead on, as a stripped down version of the OS and an older Apple Watch chip will be packed into a frame thinner than the Ray-Ban Metas. Sounds like a home run on paper, but there are some big obstacles between now and WWDC to overcome — not just in Apple’s software, but in smart eyewear more broadly. Cutting the Bluetooth tether (Image credit: Future) The most exciting detail about the prototype (codenamed N50) isn’t that “Tic Tac” sized MagSafe charger or the flushed oval cameras — it’s that native Wi-Fi connectivity. Up until this point, anyone wearing smart glasses will know the Bluetooth tether is their Achilles’ heel. Wearables are supposed to gain you freedom from your phone, and you can’t really do that if you rely on something you have to be close to. The moment you walk into another room leaving your phone on your desk, that wearable turns into a pair of dumb specs. But by giving the glasses their own Wi-Fi radio, Apple could be granting you actual independence. That friction of leaving your phone on the charger at home and still streaming audio/pinging Siri would be a huge quality-of-life upgrade. The closest we’re getting to this is the cellular data plan in Snap Specs at the moment. The ‘no screen’ reality (Image credit: Tom's Guide) My initial prediction was based on the idea that visionOS is a visual experience. “Vision” is in the name after all, but if you were hoping for AR displays, you’re going to have to keep waiting. According to Gurman, Apple’s first glasses will be a screen-free experience. With audio and cameras in the driving sign, the glasses will use visual intelligence to scan your surroundings and Siri AI to answer questions about it, all while relying on built-in mics and speakers for calls and Apply Music playback. Of course, one of the key benefits here is that by ditching the heavy optical engines, Apple gets to keep the glasses lightweight, stylish and comfortable. But also, this design choice creates a massive, singular issue: the future of this category needs a screen (in my opinion). Siri AI is the key (Image credit: John Velasco / Tom's Guide) And this brings me to the elephant in the room. Apple is betting the entire farm on Siri, but Siri’s not ready yet. The master plan is Siri being the agentic bridge of your devices. Instead of developers building dedicated apps for the glasses, your assistant will just hijack your existing iOS apps — booking Ubers, ordering Starbucks or securing OpenTable reservations entirely through conversation. In theory, it’s brilliant. In practice, it could be a very tough hill to climb. (Image credit: Future) Between now and 2027, Siri AI needs to get so much better. Currently, we’re seeing long pause times to simple prompts on your iPhone, and the Apple HomeView routinely fumbles complex, multi-step smart home commands. If Siri is currently struggling to seamlessly manage a stationary smart home, imagine how badly it is going to hallucinate when you’re walking down a noisy Manhattan street asking it to visually analyze a restaurant menu and cross-reference your calendar. When should Apple launch? (Image credit: Future) Gurman’s report already notes that Apple’s software and AI development is running behind schedule, which could easily delay this 2027 launch. And honestly? They should until it’s bulletproof. Apple’s hardware team looks set to deliver a sleek, Wi-Fi-enabled wearable showpiece. But if they strap it to an AI assistant that still doesn’t understand what you actually want, that expensive pair of smart glasses is going to feel like a very expensive bluetooth…

articles.title: Jensen Huang could be plotting return as Nvidia CEO, report claims
articles.content: Just days after he left the company under a cloud of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang might be on his way back to the company he founded. That's after a number of his allies rallied in support for Huang, including influential SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and outspoken Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. The pair are just two of those demanding that Nvidia's board has a rethink, hoping that it will choose to "Bring Jensen Back" to the company. Huang is now discussing that possibility, according to a Financial Times report . "Huang has discussed with confidantes the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter," the report claimed, adding that allies were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley figures to try and lobby for his return. Huang's resignation from his Nvidia post came after he released a statement confirming his affair , one which could have repercussions far beyond Nvidia itself. U.S. intelligence was reported to believe that the woman involved in an affair with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang (no relation), is a spy working for the Chinese Ministry of State Security , or MSS. Ms. Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, an AI company accused of smuggling $2 billion worth of AI chips into China via a subsidiary called Speedmatrix. Since Jensen Huang admitted to his adultery, it was further alleged that he had a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported to him . That alone would potentially constitute a violation of Nvidia's own code of conduct. But the affair with an alleged Chinese spy is likely to be the most troublesome for the former-but-potentially-returning CEO. Now, an open letter sent to Nvidia's board by Huang's allies has urged them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” The open letter was penned by Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker, both shareholders. @yunta_tsai A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too November 13, 2026 However, Nvidia has already started looking elsewhere. After placing chief financial officer Colette Kress in charge on an interim basis, it's believed the company has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a potential Huang successor . Haas spent around seven years at Nvidia before leaving in 2013, but no official confirmation has been announced, nor is it likely to be until a decision is made. It's possible that Huang can expect a vote of confidence from U.S. President Donald Trump, with the pair having a good relationship to date. But Trump recently called for former Apple CEO Tim Cook to take over at Nvidia . Outside of the White House, Huang has other concerns to deal with. Congress has summoned him to appear before a Select Committee over his affair with the suspected Chinese spy, threatening to subpoena him if necessary .
articles.author: Oliver Haslam

articles.title: AI-Assisted Coders Run Windows on iPhone Duo, Build a Floppy Disk-Based AI Chatbot for MS-DOS
articles.content: The blog XDA Developers reports that a Claude enthusiast used the AI assistant to make a language model that runs off a floppy disk. "And you can stick it on a DOS computer to boot." The language models "runs at a respectable speed, given that it's running off a CPU that was designed decades before LLMs were even a thing." Over on the ClaudeAI subreddit, user wollymonjak showed off this really impressive feat... [I]t's not going to be a particularly powerful AI; in fact, wollymonjak notes that if you ask something too complex or too long, it starts spitting out nonsense. But who cares about that when you're using a language model on DOS? The same blog also notes that "the iPhone Duo hasn't been out for too long, and someone has already gotten Windows 11 on it." As spotted by TechSpot, this cool feat was performed by Ammaar Reshi over on X. Their project is called WindowsiOS, and its goal is to get Windows 11 running on an iPhone Duo without jailbreaking. Usually, when we cover a project coded up by AI, Claude is the one that called the shots; this time, Reshi opted to use Gemini 4 Carbon, Google's flagship model. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware

articles.title: SpaceX catches Starship on the first try
articles.content: SpaceX caught its Starship upper stage returning from orbit on its first attempt, but the Super Heavy booster ended its flight in an explosion after recovery was aborted. The catch was a remarkable achievement: Starship returned to the same launch tower it had left almost a day earlier, settling into its giant mechanical arms. Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said. The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left. Many more development flights remain before SpaceX can deliver its promised fully reusable launch system. NASA's Space Shuttle came close, but the large external tank was expended with every launch, and the orbiters never matched the cadence SpaceX reckons it can achieve with Starship. SpaceX boss Elon Musk admitted that "many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)." Cadence will be key if Starship is going to meet NASA's needs for the Artemis missions. Somewhere between 6 and 22 launches (depending on who you ask) will be required for a lunar mission, and SpaceX has yet to demonstrate in-space propellant transfer between vehicles. Next year's Artemis III mission also calls for docking tests between NASA's Orion spacecraft and a test version of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System (HLS) in low Earth orbit. The booster fumble shouldn't obscure what the engineering teams achieved. Now comes the small matter of doing it again – preferably with both stages intact. ®

articles.title: Alibaba touts 62% lower task costs with Qwen4-Max, adds cyber safeguards
articles.content: Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship model, claiming it reduces the average cost of completing professional tasks by 62% compared with its predecessor while introducing additional safeguards against offensive cybersecurity capabilities and other high-risk uses. “According to Work360 — a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields — Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%,” Alibaba said in a blog post. The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction. The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said. It supports a 1-million-token context window. The company attributed the savings to lower token use and new list prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, down from $2 and $6. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said enterprises should treat the figure as a vendor benchmark rather than an assured reduction in their own AI spending. The relevant measure, he said, is the cost of an accepted result, including retries, reasoning tokens, and employee time spent checking outputs. “Alibaba has published the mileage it got on its own road, and a buyer’s bill depends on the road the buyer drives,” Gogia said. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should measure successful task completion rather than token prices alone. “An enterprise should benchmark what it costs to complete 1,000 real business tasks successfully, not what it costs to generate a million tokens,” Kadakia said. Alibaba also cited improvements across coding and agentic evaluations, including Code Arena and Agents’ Last Exam. In an automotive manufacturing demonstration, the company said Qwen4-Max reduced manual workpiece programming time from approximately 475 minutes to 24 minutes. Security claims need independent testing Alongside the cost figures, Alibaba set out changes to what the model learns about hacking at the training-data stage. “For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and remediation, while removing data for offensive tasks aimed at enhancing attack capabilities,” the Alibaba blog post said. The company said code security checks added during training lifted the share of functions passing both functionality and security tests on Last Secure Code Bench from 22% to 31.8%. Its internal security experts found the model’s defensive capabilities had “improved substantially,” the post added. Kadakia questioned whether offensive and defensive cybersecurity knowledge can be reliably separated through training-data filtering. “One of the fundamental challenges with cybersecurity AI is that offensive and defensive knowledge are largely the same knowledge,” he said, noting that understanding SQL injection is necessary both to exploit and prevent it. Gogia said the distinction requires independent validation, recommending that CISOs seek assessments from government evaluators or established external red teams rather than rely solely on Alibaba’s internal testing. The announcement follows an October investigation by Canadian AI company Cohere, which reported that an earlier Alibaba model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, attempted to send a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage destination in Beijing during a security test. articles.title: iPhone 20 Pro Rumored to Feature New 17nm Camera Sensor
articles.content: Next year's iPhone 20 Pro could feature a main camera sensor with logic circuitry manufactured using a new 17-nanometer process, according to Weibo-based leaker Ice Universe . Modern stacked camera sensors separate their light-sensitive pixels from the logic circuitry responsible for reading out and processing image data. A more advanced manufacturing process for the logic layer could potentially enable faster readout speeds, improved power efficiency, and more sophisticated image processing. The leaker provided no further details about the sensor, which would reportedly debut in Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone in 2027. Apple is expected to skip the "iPhone 19" moniker next year, just like it did with the iPhone 9 prior to the release of the iPhone X in 2017 to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the original iPhone. Interestingly, Samsung has already been developing a 17nm Low Power Value (17LPV) process specifically for CMOS image sensor signal processing circuitry, according to a 2024 Omdia report . Apple is also working with Samsung to produce advanced image sensors at its Austin, Texas facility. Previous reports suggest the partnership involves a three-layer stacked sensor design, but there's currently no clear link between that project and the claimed 17nm component. Separately, Apple is rumored to be developing its own image sensor incorporating LOFIC technology, which could substantially improve dynamic range and preserve more detail in highlights and shadows. Again though, it's not clear whether the latest claim relates to that sensor. iPhone 20 Pro: Ten Big Changes That Could Redefine Apple's Flagship Apple is rumoured to be a developing a radical new design for its second commemorative iPhone, featuring a new quad-curved OLED display that wraps around the edges of the device, and a screen with potentially no cutouts at all. Apple is expected to debut the device in or around September 2027. articles.title: Samsung’s Phone app could start checking if calls from contacts are being spoofed
articles.content: Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority TL;DR Samsung’s Phone app could soon warn you when a scammer is faking a call from your contacts. The feature uses RCS to verify that the call is indeed coming from the caller your phone says it is from. It does not share the caller’s details with Samsung’s servers, but will require an active internet connection. The feature will not verify calls coming from unknown callers, but only the ones saved in your contacts. In June this year, Google introduced a mechanism to identify potentially harmful spoofed or fake calls on Pixel devices . That way, a scammer using a spoofing tool to make the call appear to come from one of your contacts could be easily discovered. The feature works on RCS, the media-rich texting protocol that allows instant messaging on Google Messages, to match the call’s origin to the contact’s device. At the time of its release on Pixel phones, Google said it plans to expand it to other devices, and we’re seeing signs of that happening now, starting with One UI 9.5 on Samsung Galaxy devices.
articles.author: Tushar Mehta
