articles.title: North America and UK are among worst for indoor mobile signal, study finds
articles.content: Ookla has found that North America, Europe, and Oceania have worse indoor mobile signal than other regions The difference in signal power can be up to around 50 times This is primarily down to these regions having poor outdoor signal in cities too If you live in North America or Europe then you’ve probably frequently found that your phone’s signal is bad indoors — but the main reason might not be what you’d assume. Ookla has carried out a study, comparing indoor and outdoor signal measurements across over 100 cities globally, and it has found that indoor signal is weakest in North America, Europe, and Oceania. But if you assumed the problem was building materials, well, you’d be — mostly — wrong. According to Ookla, the material a building is constructed from can make a difference to a signal’s ability to pass through walls, but it’s not a dramatic difference, with timber-framed buildings reducing a signal by 2 dB (decibels), while concrete ones still only drop it by 7 dB, with the median drop being 4 dB. That accounts for under a tenth of the overall difference in indoor signal between different cities and regions, with 85% of the difference coming from how good the outdoor signal is. So in other words, cities with better outdoor signal tend to have better indoor signal, too — which isn't entirely surprising. (Image credit: Ookla) A 50x difference These differences are surprisingly big, with the median indoor signal measured in the likes of Dubai, Bangkok, and Seoul being around -88 dBm (decibel-milliwatts) on 4G, whereas in Naples it’s -105 dBm and in Geneva and Birmingham it’s -104 dBm. Numbers closer to zero are better here, and that roughly -17 dBm gap is a difference of around 50 times in signal power. Overall, North American cities have a median signal of -101 dBm, with European ones similarly posting a median of -100 dBm, while in for example East Asia the median is -90 dBm — making for a much better signal. So even though your signal might not seem bad outside, it likely is if you’re getting poor indoor signal — it’s just the move to indoors decreases it ever further, making it more noticeable. The solution is for carriers to rethink their network deployment, with for example a denser deployment of masts and other infrastructure, or the use of more or better configured spectrum. Still, without changes at a government level, this probably won’t be addressed, with Ookla noting that cities and countries that have indoor-specific rules for coverage tend to perform better than those that don’t.
articles.author: James Rogerson

articles.title: Campaign to reinstate Huang as Nvidia CEO now has 175,000 signatures
articles.content: 'Stand with Jensen' petition calling for the return of Huang now has over 175,000 signatures It asks for an immediate reinstatement of Huang as Nvidia CEO and an "independent investigation and a fair hearing" regarding the matters he resigned over A separate report claims that Huang may be considering the possibility of such a return Following the exit of Nvidia's CEO last week , a petition has been put together to campaign for the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. VideoCardz noticed the 'Stand with Jensen ' website which hosts a petition and open letter that has now been signed by some 175,000 people, some of whom are high-profile names in the tech industry. That includes Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney (of Epic Games), Tobias Lutke (CEO of Shopify), Travis Kalanick (the former CEO of Uber), Steve Chen (the former CTO of YouTube) and Julien Chaumond (current CTO at Hugging Face). It's made clear that Huang himself doesn't endorse the letter. The demands laid out by the letter to the Nvidia board are threefold, including firstly that Huang should be reinstated as CEO immediately – to stabilize the situation – but if the board believes "his continued absence is necessary" that they should provide an explanation of why. The second demand is to "ensure an independent investigation and a fair hearing", and the third is to deliver a timely public explanation of what's happened and how the interests of Nvidia staff and shareholders were weighed up in this matter. The petition states: "Thirty-three years of leadership do not place anyone above accountability. But accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice." Meanwhile, given all this, a separate report from The Financial Times claims that Huang is mulling a comeback bid and the "possibility of returning" based on chatter from multiple sources. An ally of the ex-CEO said they were putting together a 'war room' of big tech executives to lobby for Huang's return (presumably including Musk and the other aforementioned names). Analysis: strong feelings and dim views (Image credit: Nvidia) Some strong feelings have been aired, then, and based on the stats from the Stand with Jensen campaign, nearly 9,000 Nvidia staff (known as 'Nvidians') are signatories of the open letter – which is 20% of the employee base. Of those employees, 26 are Vice Presidents (or Senior VPs), which is a good chunk of the top leadership (maybe approaching half of them, although there are no precise numbers for VPs at Team Green). Of course, none of this can be verified, and we have to take these numbers on trust. Looking at Reddit, there's little sympathy for Huang, particularly among PC gamers ( though his exit is arguably another distinctly negative development ). Even on the subreddits relating to Nvidia stock, there's a mostly dim view of this petition (just over half of the signatories are declared as shareholders). However, it is notable that a fair few major names in tech have signed the letter – I still doubt that this will spark a turnaround in sentiment for the board, of course. These kind of campaigns aren't known for producing much in the way of concrete results, shall we say. That said, given the 'war room' rumor from the FT, maybe the petition will give Huang a bit more impetus to launch the comeback bid that is supposedly being considered behind the scenes. If it's going to happen, it will obviously need to happen quickly. Meanwhile, the letter signatures are likely to exceed 200,000 today. In case you missed this last week (somehow), Colette Kress (who was CFO) is currently the interim CEO while Nvidia conducts a search for Huang's permanent replacement (who could come from inside or outside the company).
articles.author: Darren Allan

articles.title: What can you safely tell AI at work?
articles.content: When Bhaskar Bharat Sawant troubleshoots a software problem, an error message often provides the first clue. It can also present a dilemma: how much of that message can he safely share with AI tools? Sawant, a lead engineer and solution architect at building-products manufacturer Cornerstone Building Brands, works with legacy applications and newer technologies. GenAI can help explain an error or suggest a way forward. But the input it needs to understand the problem may expose personally identifiable information, a customer’s competitive secrets, or his own company’s proprietary information. “Logs or error messages can reveal internal service names, configuration details, or business processes,” Sawant said. “You have to protect that information whether it belongs to your employer or a customer.” A customer’s name is an obvious identifier. A method name, file path, or sequence of requests between systems is less conspicuous. Together, those details can expose how an application works or how a business operates — even when no individual can be identified. Sawant’s approach is to construct a smaller, fictional version of the problem. “I create a small code example with made-up data that reproduces the issue,” he said. “Then I ask myself whether someone outside the company could piece together proprietary information from it. If they could, I simplify it further or keep it out of the AI tool.” That process takes judgment and effort before AI can save him any time. It also exposes the difficulty behind a simple workplace instruction: don’t share confidential or sensitive information with generative AI. Employees must translate that warning into decisions about actual work, often while trying to meet a deadline. What remains after you remove the names Employees can recognize the need to protect information and still overlook what they are sharing. Julian Gage , who provides fractional data protection officer services through Engage Compliance, recalls advising a health technology company where an employee uploaded a spreadsheet containing treatment notes and clinic customer numbers to an AI service that was not company-approved. The records did not name the patients, but each customer number provided a link back to an identifiable person. “Replacing a name with a customer number doesn’t make the information anonymous,” he said. “Someone with access to the clinic’s records could still establish whose treatment notes they were.” Meeting transcripts present a similar problem. Removing a colleague’s name may accomplish little if the discussion describes an absence, medical treatment, or other circumstances that make the person recognizable. “You have to look at the content, not just the names,” Gage said. “If people can connect the dots and identify the individual, you haven’t made the information anonymous.” Attachments introduce further opportunities to miss something. Screenshots can include identifying details outside the passage an employee wants analyzed. Spreadsheets can contain hidden columns that remain in the uploaded file. Automated connections can send meeting transcripts to an AI service before anyone has reviewed or redacted them. Sawant tackles that problem by first investigating the error himself, then deciding whether he can describe it safely to an outside AI service. “I start by reproducing the problem in a controlled development environment, examining the error details, and isolating the component causing trouble,” he said. “If passing the problem to an outside AI service requires too much sensitive context, I continue troubleshooting with internal resources rather than sharing that information.” Even after taking these precautions, an employee may still need to complete the task without AI. Approved for what? Company-provided tools appear to offer a way out of the trade-off. Employees can retain the context, work within an approved environment, and get on with the task. articles.title: Last week’s Microsoft Outlook outage turned a hotel pool fault into a hospital trip for 15 guests
articles.content: TL;DR Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany were reportedly hurt after a faulty dosing system pumped too much chlorine into the hotel pool. The pool’s safety system sent a warning by email, but staff never received it because of last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage. Microsoft says the outage was caused by a problem from an earlier network capacity upgrade, and it has promised a full post-incident report. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage did more than keep people out of their inboxes. In Germany it played a part in a chemical incident that sent hotel guests to the hospital. German public broadcaster WDR reported that on Friday, November 13, a fault in the automatic chlorine dosing system at Hotel Ling Bao pushed far too much chlorine into the hotel’s pool. The hotel belongs to the Phantasialand theme park in Brühl, near Cologne.

articles.title: Datacenters' share of UK planning applications nearly triples in three years
articles.content: Datacenters made up nearly three times as large a share of UK planning applications in the year to September 2026 as they did three years earlier, with councils receiving 59 submissions. The figures come from planning data site Plota, whose Q3 2026 Planning Index draws on applications from every council across the UK. Plota has logged 416 datacenter applications since 2016, though these include extensions and alterations, not just new bit barns. Estimates put Britain's existing fleet at between 477 and 602 facilities. The peak for volume came in the 12 months to March 2021, when 63 campus applications were filed. However, overall planning applications were also higher then, so datacenters accounted for just 1.1 in every 10,000 filed. In the current period they equate to 1.4 in every 10,000. The figures show that applications for building new server halls are about as high as they have been over the past decade, and close to their recent peak as a share of all applications. Even so, the application numbers don't show the dramatic jump that the steady stream of bit barn announcements might suggest. Nor do they tell us how many facilities are actually being built. Applications did bounce around the middle of 2024, when the current government - and its fetish for all things AI - was elected. But it didn't publish the AI Opportunities Action Plan , which recommended "AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning to speed up datacenter builds, until the start of 2025. Plota links the rise to datacenters being recognized as critical national infrastructure (CNI) in September 2024, and a December 2024 update to the planning framework that told councils to identify suitable sites for them. The facilities are getting larger. One site being built for Equinix near London's M25 motorway will feature three data halls with more than 250 MW capacity, while another planned for Havering in East London could go up to 600 MW. Both were billed as being among Europe's largest campuses. According to Plota, just 3.3 percent of datacenter applications decided between 2016 and 2024 were refused, against 11.3 percent across all applications. The government has also overturned some local council refusals, controversially, as at a site near Abbots Langley in Hertfordshire last year. Slough leads Plota's tally of applications since 2016 with 28, followed by Tower Hamlets in East London with 16, Leeds with 12, and West Northamptonshire with 11. Developers in England can also ask ministers to bring qualifying datacenter projects into the nationally significant infrastructure planning regime , shifting the consent decision from the council to central government. Projects taking that route fall outside Plota's council-based figures. A recent report found UK ministers met with representatives from 137 different businesses between July 2024 and June 2026 to discuss datacenters, while there were no meetings with environmental or community groups about them. ®

articles.title: Delivery drones are coming. For some with PTSD, that's a terrifying prospect.
articles.content: In August, Amazon announced plans to expand its Prime Air delivery drone program to “ nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026 ." Combined with similar uncrewed aerial delivery programs from DoorDash and Zipline (in partnership with Uber and Walmart), the expansion suggests that flying robots dropping their payloads onto suburban lawns will soon be commonplace. For many people, delivery drones will be little more than a novelty, occasionally good for a laugh when one does something ridiculous. For others, though, their growing use could be a nightmare. As the instant delivery industry clears the last FAA hurdles to rapid deliveries beyond an operator's line of sight, an increasing number of people worldwide are living with post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders triggered by drones. The use of all manner of weaponized drones in the ongoing war in Ukraine and in Israeli attacks on Lebanon and Gaza has already produced an epidemic of what some mental health professionals have dubbed “dronophobia. ” And while relatively few US troops have been targeted by drones flown by Iran, ISIS, and Iran-backed militias throughout the Middle East, even those who have not directly been attacked may experience anxiety simply because of the ample video footage of attacks circulating in news and social media. articles.title: In The AI Era, Keep Hiring New College Grads — And Make Them Managers From Day One
articles.content: A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI. Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?” The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children? College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic , a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening. What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that. Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams. The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution. The craft of management The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong. Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management. These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives , naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers. It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win. I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management. The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner. When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage. What happens without management This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident . Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face . In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed…

articles.title: Grab a beginner-friendly Anycubic 3D printer for under $300, back at its record-low price
articles.content: You can pick up a serious discount on an Anycubic 3D printer right now. The Anycubic Kobra X is on sale at Amazon for $299.99, back down to its lowest ever price on Amazon . This 17% discount nets you a printer that scored you one of our Editor's Choic awards, along with a four and a half star score in our Anycubic Kobra X review . ● Check out this 3D printer deal on Amazon This is an entry-level printer with a lot of potential for beginners and pros. Its multi-material ACE Gen 2 system is built in, meaning you don't have to worry about pausing your printer to switch out colors. Our testing saw that, with a four-color print with 776 color swaps, the Anycubic Kobra X was 10 hours faster than the Bambu Lab A1, despite otherwise-similar printing speeds (and a very similar design). If you want more complex, multi-colored prints, this is the better option. Kobra X Multicolor 3D Printer: was $359 now $299 All-time low price The Kobra X delivers fast, affordable multicolor printing without a complicated external AMS or premium price tag. It features a 260 x 260 x 260mm (10.23 x 10.23 x 10.23-inch) build volume, automatic + Z bed leveling, and a color touch screen. View Deal This printer, which launched earlier this year, even supports additional ACE Gen 2 systems; you can connect up to four to it, meaning you can manage prints with up to 19 different colors. Our review found it to be a fairly quiet printer during use, requiring very little filament retraction, and it worked flawlessly printing with a range of different materials. It also has a 49-point full auto leveling system, along with an RFID tag reader, which will work with Anycubic filaments to help it quickly identify what filament you're using. It has a build volume of 260 x 260 x 260 mm (10.23 x 10.23 x 10.23 in), ships with a direct drive extruder, and comes with a range of options to connect and manage it, including over USB using the built-in touch screen, via a network connection, or by using the app or cloud service. There's also a 720p camera to help you with real-time monitoring and for error alerts, along with AI-driven anti-foreign object and spaghetti detection to quickly alert you if there's a print issue. The $299.99 sale price for this Anycubic Kobra X 3D printer makes it a great option for a beginner looking to start printing, or a pro looking for a second printer for multi-colored models. It's back down to a record low price for Amazon Prime members, so you'll need to be signed in and have an active Prime membership to get this Anycubic printer at this discounted price.

For beginners, no other camera is better than the Canon EOS R100, and it's currently down to just $499 at Amazon . This bundle comes with the 18-45mm lens which is perfect to get you started. If you're a vlogger, the Canon EOS R50 V and the 14-30mm lens is $200 off at Amazon right now , and I awarded this camera a 4.5-star rating in my review . Street and travel photographers should grab the Fujifilm X-T50, which is $100 off at Amazon , while professionals should consider the Canon EOS R6 Mark III, which is also discounted by $200 at Adorama . articles.title: Check your iPhone Duo delivery date — a bunch of orders just jumped the line
articles.content: Anyone still waiting on an iPhone Duo pre-order from the Apple Store may want to check their delivery dates . Because your foldable might be arriving a little earlier than Apple originally promised. That's what various users on the MacRumors forums have been saying, anyway. The most excitable of users have posted about how their initial arrival estimate was in late January, but over the last few days it seems to have changed to mid-to-late December instead. One user noted that they ordered two Duos on pre-order day, five minutes apart. The first arrived on launch day (October 23), while the other had a January 25 delivery estimate — which has just changed to the same mid-December window. Some users even posted screenshots of their delivery estimate moving to mid November — which is right around now. What's happening? (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Obviously, the question of why Apple has suddenly changed these delivery estimates is being discussed at great length. Some speculate that this could be down to Apple narrowing down when it can actually deliver iPhone Duos, since pre-order delivery estimates defaulted to January extremely quickly. Others speculate that it could be the fact that more people have been cancelling pre-orders for some reason or another. There are reasons why that might be the case, such as picking the phone up from a third party retailer able to deliver sooner than Apple. Alternatively, others may have decided the iPhone Duo isn't for them. Whether that's down to the cost, the lengthy wait times, or the issues with broken screens , is unclear. However, canceled pre-orders mean that other people move up the line and get their units faster. Similarly any Duos that are returned unopened, possibly failed scalpers or anyone with buyer's remorse, will likely be put back into circulation. Anyone ordering an iPhone Duo from Apple right now will still be stuck with a January 22 delivery date. Still, with the new year coming up fast, it's not as bad a prospect as it was back when pre-orders opened. articles.title: Enterprises to pay up to 20% more for Microsoft cloud services in some countries
articles.content: Microsoft is slated to raise commercial cloud prices in several markets, with customers in India and New Zealand facing the steepest price hikes. The changes, which are set to take effect from January 1, 2027, will increase commercial cloud prices by 15.7% in India and 10% in New Zealand, the company wrote in a blog post announcing its annual local currency pricing adjustments to account for foreign exchange fluctuations. The annual local currency pricing adjustments follow Microsoft’s announcement in July , wherein it said that it would move to an annual process for adjusting local currency prices for commercial cloud services. Under the new approach, adjustments are expected to take place every January, with customers and partners notified in advance each November. The pricing changes also extend to some on-premises offerings, with Indian customers facing increases of up to 20% and those in New Zealand facing a 10% hike, according to the blog post. Higher prices could squeeze enterprise IT budgets This change in prices, particularly for Microsoft’s India customers, is “significant because it outpaces most enterprises’ annual IT budget growth,” said Manoj Chandra Jha , principal analyst at Nord-IQ Research. “That means the adjustments are likely to result in a real cut in spending power for those enterprises rather than a rounding error. The hardest hit will be organizations heavily standardized on Microsoft, particularly in sectors such as BFSI, IT services, global capability centers (GCCs), and large-scale manufacturing,” Jha added. “Within those, the workloads most exposed are the ones with constant, heavy usage: Microsoft 365 seats at scale, data and analytics platforms, and Azure-based AI,” he further added. Innovation projects could bear the brunt of higher costs That additional pressure on IT budgets is also likely to come at the expense of discretionary technology spending. “Enterprises are likely to delay or shelve innovation projects, particularly AI pilots, to accommodate higher operating costs, meaning CIOs will end up spending more only to keep what they already run, with little room left for new initiatives,” Jha said. Further, the recurring nature of these annual price adjustments could also push CIOs to reconsider their dependence on Microsoft and explore ways to diversify their technology investments, according to Pareekh Jain , principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting. “AWS and Google Cloud could become more attractive, particularly if they can offer more competitive and predictable pricing. However, this is more likely to apply to new deployments, as migrating existing workloads away from Microsoft can be expensive and complex,” Jain said. Similarly, higher on-premises prices could act as a catalyst for cloud migration decisions among CIOs, particularly those using Windows Server, SQL Server, and other Microsoft infrastructure products, as higher licensing and maintenance costs could make moving workloads to the cloud more attractive, Jain said. However, he cautioned that enterprises should compare the “full lifecycle costs of on-premises, hybrid and cloud alternatives” as moving to the cloud is “not automatically cheaper always.” Some ways to optimize costs Meanwhile, in the short term, CIOs could look to optimize existing Microsoft deployments and renegotiate licensing agreements to offset some of the additional costs, Jha pointed out. “Removing unused Microsoft 365 seats, moving staff off E5 licenses they don’t need, and right-sizing idle Azure resources can often offset much of the increase on their own,” Jha said. “Beyond that, enterprises should renew before January 1 to lock in current rates and push for price protection in their enterprise agreements. Steady workloads should go on reserved instances or savings plans, while new workloads are placed wherever the economics work best,” Jha added. In addition, CIOs will need to account for potential currency fluctuations when forecasting technology…

articles.title: New Apple TV 4K's A19 Chip Has One Core Switched Off
articles.content: Apple's new Apple TV 4K uses an A19 chip with one efficiency core disabled, according to system diagnostic data shared by code explorer pdfu . That suggests a five-core CPU with two performance cores and three efficiency cores, compared with the six-core CPU in the iPhone 17. The reported maximum clock speeds are 4.26GHz for performance cores and 2.592GHz for efficiency cores, with a five-core GPU reaching 1.47GHz. (These are maximum frequencies, not measurements of sustained performance.) Apple is likely using binned chips, where the disabled core is defective. The company used a similar configuration in the 2022 Apple TV 4K , whose A15 chip also had one CPU core disabled. articles.title: Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia
articles.content: Elon Musk and a bunch of Silicon Valley heavyweights want Jensen Huang back at Nvidia, and they've decided an online petition is the way to make it happen. An open letter addressed to Nvidia's board had attracted more than 173,000 signatures at the time of writing, just four days after Huang's departure following revelations about his personal relationships, including an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China. The campaign, launched under the banner "Stand with Jensen," calls on Nvidia to reinstate its co-founder and former CEO while an independent investigation establishes the facts, give him a chance to respond to the allegations, and publicly explain why he was forced out. "For thirty-three years, Jensen poured his heart and soul into building Nvidia," the letter reads. "He bet it on ideas that most of the industry dismissed, carried it through years when the bets looked foolish, and stayed long enough to see them change how the world computes. "Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took. This company is the work of his life. That deserves more than gratitude after the fact. It deserves fairness now." Among the supporters are Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator boss Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. More than 8,000 signatories also identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to roughly a fifth of its workforce. However, how many of those signatures are genuine is anyone's guess. The site doesn't verify names or employers, so there's nothing stopping someone from signing as Musk, Huang, or Nvidia's entire board if they fancy it. The campaign follows Huang's resignation on November 12 , ending his 33-year reign at the GPU giant he co-founded in 1993. His departure came after reports of an affair with Alice Huang , a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who US intelligence suspects of spying for Beijing, and a separate alleged relationship with an Nvidia employee. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress has been handed the unenviable job of running the company while its board searches for a permanent replacement. Huang's departure has left the chipmaker facing something of an identity crisis , with rivals undoubtedly watching the chaos with interest. Huang himself may not be ready to hang up his leather jacket. According to the Financial Times , the former CEO has discussed a possible comeback with associates, while an ally is reportedly assembling a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. The effort could even involve seeking support from the White House, although Washington appears rather less enthusiastic about the prospect. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs a "dramatic shake-up" and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also wants answers about whether Nvidia knowingly allowed advanced AI chips to reach China in breach of US export restrictions. None of that seems to have put off Huang's supporters. "He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company," Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick said. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, giving investors their first major opportunity to grill management about the leadership crisis. Whether the board will be swayed by a petition full of unverified names is another matter. Running one of the world's most valuable companies is, after all, not supposed to be a popularity contest. ®

articles.title: Fable 5.2 creates an underwater world in a browser in only 96 KB
articles.content: Claude Fable 5.2 was released recently to mostly rave reviews, with both users and analysis outlets ranking it nipping at the heels of the much pricier Opus 5.5. Perhaps as practical proof of that claim, front-end developer Maksymilian Dendura took inspiration from the demoscene and had Fable roll his own virtual underwater world, Abyssal Garden , in only 96 KB of Javascript/HTML — you can check it out here . The demo's 3D space and textures are all procedurally generated, meaning they're the result of mathematical equations rather than prebuilt 3D meshes, and all calculated on load. Using actual meshes and images for textures would otherwise take up a significant amount of space. Building structures procedurally is difficult and has limitations, but it's exceedingly effective when used properly. Some games employ this technique for repeated elements like trees and grass. Likewise, all the visual effects and even some texturing are done with shaders, which are small programs that change how a mesh or texture appears — for example, to make parts of an object shiny. Games use them extensively, as many players are aware, thanks to endless "loading shaders" screens or Unreal Engine's st-tu-tutering. The result is definitely impressive, especially but not only as it's purely browser-based, relying on WebGPU and WebGL. Both are rarely-mentioned technologies that have actually existed for a long while now . As their names imply, they let developers render 2D and 3D graphics in a manner similar to that of OpenGL, but in a browser, using JavaScript as the base language. The demo's most impressive fact is the simplicity of the prompt that got Fable 5.2 to build it. It's only about 40 lines long with word wrapping, and clearly illustrates the degree of autonomy that contemporary agentic AI has when given a specific, yet exceedingly open-ended task like this one. It's reasonable enough to assume the author did a few rounds of tweaking (and he has excellent artistic taste too), but the agent's acumen is nevertheless impressive. Comparing this demo to an actual game is inevitable, but the reality is that demos have but an atom-sized fraction of the content of a full game, and are limited to little or no interaction, logic, or physics. Performance is decent for what is a great-looking but otherwise tiny and almost featureless space. The author says that he's getting 180 FPS at 1440p on an RTX 5070 Ti. Likewise, having this world in 97 KB sounds impressive, but it's actually gigantic for this type of demo, even if an X user further optimized it for 52 KB. Regular computing users, including AI neophytes and acolytes, may not be aware that this kind of space-optimized programming for the purposes of visual/aural demonstrations is a discipline and art form that harkens back to the 1980s when 16-bit computers appeared — called the " demoscene ." By no means discounting the extraordinary fact that Fable did this nearly all by itself — which is the actual achievement here — code wizards have pulled off nearly impossible feats decades ago, including in browsers. The 2009 demo Elevatedn (17 years ago) has a comparable aesthetic, and includes music, in just under 4 KB (yes, four). There's even a browser version of it, taking up all of 4,777 bytes. Hartverdrahtet (2012 — 14 years ago) has a highly complex 3D space, again in 4 KB. And old-timers in the audience will remember ".kkrieger", an FPS game prototype that fit in all of 96 KB, including meshes, textures, music, and sound effects... back in 2004 .
articles.author: Bruno Ferreira

articles.title: Grab a DDR5 gaming PC with a 10GB GPU for only $949
articles.content: Pick up a budget gaming PC with 10GB of dedicated GPU VRAM. The iBuypower Slate Gaming PC with Intel Arc B570 graphics is just $949 at Best Buy in today's deal. Saving you $250 off its $1,199.99 list price, this deal is the perfect way to get into PC gaming on a strict budget, and costs less than a Steam Machine and some handheld gaming consoles. ● Check out this deal at Best Buy This iBuypower Slate gaming PC comes with a 10-core, 10-thread Intel Core Ultra 5 225F processor, an Intel Arc B570 graphics card with 10GB of VRAM, 16GB of DDR5 memory, and a 1TB NVMe SSD for storage. With the current pricing trend for DDR5 memory and PC components in general, this is an effective combination of parts for a 1080p gaming rig without breaking the bank. Slate Gaming PC (Arc B570): was $1199.99 now $949 This frugal machine features an Intel Core Ultra 5 225F processor and an Intel Arc B570 graphics card with 10GB of VRAM. There's also 16GB of DDR5 memory and a 1TB NVMe SSD for storage. View Deal The standout component of this PC is the Intel B570 graphics card, which comes with a generous 10GB of VRAM. For 1080p gaming, 10GB of VRAM is a good amount to handle the textures and shaders on high and ultra settings. However, on higher settings it will start to struggle in 1440p gaming when that VRAM gets swallowed up and starts using the CPU to compensate. The chart below from our rasterization benchmarking game suite highlights the performance of the B570, and has it sitting in the middle of the pack, competing closely with Nvidia's 12GB RTX 3060. Check out our Intel Arc B570 review for more detailed information on this GPU's performance and other metrics. Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Thanks to the skyrocketing price of memory and storage, buying a prebuilt gaming PC is now a much cheaper way to own your own gaming PC rather than trying to construct your own. PC builders like iBuypower are able to grab these parts much cheaper than normal consumers and can offset some of the price rises with their stocks of components and buying power. Don't expect prices of prebuilt PCs to stay low, however, as the market continues to see prices go up as available memory stocks diminish. For just $949, this is a superb deal for a starter gaming PC if you're just getting into PC gaming. The B570 may be a budget graphics card, but it has come a long way since launch, thanks to driver optimizations and compatibility with more games, so you're now getting more bang for your buck with this GPU.

articles.title: Apple Seeks 200,000 People for AI Health Study
articles.content: Apple on Sunday announced the launch of an Apple Health AI Usage Study that gives participants access to a dedicated iPhone app that answers everyday health questions using medical research and, optionally, their own Health app data. Conducted in collaboration with clinical AI company OpenEvidence, the U.S.-only study will examine how people understand and evaluate AI-generated health information, what makes them trust it, and whether it can help them prepare for appointments with their doctors. "At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life," said Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness. "Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey." The app combines OpenEvidence's technology with an Apple-designed research experience, where responses include links to peer-reviewed clinical sources, with information drawn from publications like The New England Journal of Medicine , JAMA , and Nature . Apple says the app presents complex medical information in approachable language. Participants can choose to share data such as their resting heart rate, activity, sleep, and lab results through HealthKit. The idea is for it to allow researchers to explore whether incorporating personal health information makes answers more relevant and easier to understand. Apple says the app can also help users put Health data in context, understand symptoms or conditions, and build personalized exercise or meal plans. Users can rate responses and complete occasional surveys about their experience, and all questions undergo processing designed to remove identifying information before reaching OpenEvidence, which deletes question-and-response data within 24 hours. Apple says study data will not be used to train AI models, and participants control whether they share HealthKit metrics or survey responses. "Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds," said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF's professor and chair of the Department of Medicine. "When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly. Connecting these tools, and rigorously studying what works, is how we'll get there." Apple is keen to stress that health tools powered by large language models can give incomplete or unclear answers, and the app includes safeguards that are meant to detect certain concerning questions and direct users toward a healthcare provider or other resources. The study isn't intended to diagnose or treat conditions, or replace advice from medical professionals. The study is open to up to 200,000 eligible U.S. residents aged 21 and older with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running iOS 26 or later. If you're eligible and interested, download the Apple Health AI Study App from the App Store to learn more. articles.title: Gemini Live could soon let you add Pikachu, Thanksgiving effects to your camera view
articles.content: Credit: Rita El Khoury / Android Authority TL;DR An Android Authority teardown has revealed that Google could add video effects to Gemini Live’s camera view. We’ve uncovered Thanksgiving, Pikachu, and Custom video effects, although none of these are working right now. Code shows that the Thanksgiving effect will offer an autumn theme with pumpkins, while the Pikachu option will show an animated 3D Pikachu. Gemini Live is one of the most cutting-edge AI features today, featuring virtually real-time conversations and the ability to share your camera or screen with the chatbot. However, it looks like Google is getting ready to have some fun with it via AI-powered video effects. APK teardown: This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship. We conducted a teardown of the Google app for Android (v17.75.23) and manually enabled a new feature called Genie, although it could also be a codename. In any event, Genie would allow users to add video effects to the live camera feed in Gemini Live. Check out our strings below.

articles.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
articles.content: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis. In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work. In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling. What You Will Learn: How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects Register now for this free webinar!

articles.title: The solution to the data center energy crisis might be in your home
articles.content: What if the solution to the energy crunch exacerbated by data center expansion wasn’t building more power plants—and investing in gas turbines and dirty fossil fuel power—but instead, simply upgrading people’s homes? A number of advocates and clean energy wonks believe there’s another way forward. By creating choreographed networks of batteries and smart devices, called virtual power plants (VPPs), utilities can lower power usage and create a well of excess power they can unleash during periods of high demand. Batteries can store energy during off-peak hours to deploy later, and smart thermostats can cut air conditioning by a few degrees to moderate periods of high usage. All could be paid for by leveraging the billions of dollars being spent by the energy-hungry data center sector. “This is a bridging technology, one that can help remake the American energy system,” says Chris Walker, vice president of power and platforms for Grid Alternatives. It’s one of the nation’s largest nonprofit clean energy providers, and it’s working on pilots seeking to prove this approach can work at scale. “We’re hearing more and more sort of advocacy for this approach, not least because you know the data center developers really need social license, but because communities are demanding actual benefits from this,” he adds. Home renovations may seem like an inadequate solution to the massive, and growing, energy footprint of data centers. The demand is unprecedented; Goldman Sachs predicted that data center energy use would more than double from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 66 gigawatts by 2027. (For comparison, 66 gigawatts is enough to power more than 50 million homes.) Increasing power generation by constructing new gas power plants is costly, both financially and environmentally, and takes time; gas turbine deliveries are backed up until 2028. It’s also broadly unpopular. Americans widely rejected data center development during the 2026 midterm election cycle, when energy costs were a constant refrain. But by using the money set to be spent on the data center energy build-out, and instead electrifying homes, adding batteries and installing solar, advocates argue it’s possible to create a distributed power system. This web of decentralized generating and power storage sites can cut energy bills, quickly create excess grid capacity that can be utilized by data centers, and build a better electrical system. It’s also much quicker to get running. These virtual power plants can be stood up in months, and at less cost. “You’re setting up a win-win solution where a hyperscaler is able to make investments in communities that make their lives better, and they’re able to get something valuable to them in return, which is speed to power,” says Annie Gilleo, vice president of the Ad Hoc Group, an energy industry consultancy. “If we’re aligning interests with the hyperscaler, the sky is the limit.” The virtual power plant experiment A number of pilots and programs are testing how to dispatch and measure distributed power systems. When proven and scaled up, this is the kind of technology that may be able to support an additional data center without requiring new power generation. In April in Minnesota, the state’s public utilities commission approved a $430 million utility-owned, battery-based virtual power plant, called the Capacity*Connect program. Xcel Energy, the local utility, will work with Sparkfund, a utility services company, to deploy 200 megawatts of small batteries across homes, local businesses, and nonprofits. These will help store energy to be used during periods of high demand. In Virginia, Google is partnering with Voltus, a distributed energy platform, to create a 1 gigawatt virtual power plant. Announced in June and recently expanded, this system will consist of a network of flexible power assets—batteries, smart thermostats, even adjustable industrial processes at factories—that can be tapped into during times…

articles.title: Sola Security Brings Prof. Randall Balestriero on Board to Explore World Models for Cybersecurity
articles.content: The next stage of enterprise cybersecurity may depend on a capability that goes beyond identifying threats: understanding how an organization's technology environment works as a connected system. A compromised identity, for example, can create risks that extend beyond the account itself. Determining which workloads it can access, how its permissions interact with infrastructure, and what could happen if those permissions are revoked requires an understanding of relationships across an enterprise environment. Sola Security believes this kind of contextual understanding could shape the next generation of cybersecurity agents. In a press release announcing its latest research appointment, the company said it has brought Prof. Randall Balestriero onto its scientific advisory board to advance that vision. Balestriero is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Brown University and a visiting researcher at Meta AI Research (FAIR). He has worked alongside renowned AI researcher Yann LeCun and co-authored research with him . His work focuses on self-supervised learning and representation learning, including how AI systems develop structured representations of the world around them. At Sola, he will advise on research directions that connect these foundational AI concepts with the everyday challenges of enterprise security. The Problem With Treating Security Findings in Isolation Enterprise security environments contain interconnected identities, permissions, workloads, and infrastructure dependencies. Yet many security questions cannot be answered by examining a single suspicious event or configuration. Identifying a compromised identity, for instance, does not automatically reveal the full extent of its access. Security teams need to understand which workloads that identity can reach and how its permissions relate to other components. The response itself can introduce additional operational considerations. Revoking access may affect other systems or workloads, making it important to understand what could break before implementing a change. This creates a distinction between detecting a security problem and understanding its implications. Sola's approach centers on the idea that AI agents need a continuously updated representation of the environments they protect. Instead of processing disconnected findings, agents should be able to understand how different components relate and evaluate the potential consequences of proposed actions. What World Models Could Bring to Cybersecurity The concept of world models is central to Sola's research direction. The company sees new types of models capable of understanding environments and relationships as a potential foundation for more advanced cybersecurity agents. Applied to enterprise security, these principles could help AI systems build comprehensive representations of organizational environments. An agent could potentially reason about how identities connect to workloads, what permissions actually enable, and how a security intervention might affect other parts of an organization. This would change the role of an AI security agent. Rather than simply responding to an alert, an agent with a deeper understanding of its environment could evaluate different possible actions and consider their downstream effects. The objective is to make decisions with greater awareness of operational context. For example, an agent identifying a compromised identity would need to do more than flag the account. It would need to understand the identity's potential reach, assess the consequences of removing its access, and determine an appropriate response. That distinction is important as enterprises increasingly introduce AI agents into security operations, where investigating threats, managing access, and carrying out remediation actions can involve interconnected systems. articles.title: Meet Meta’s JiTTests: LLM-Generated Tests Designed to Fail Before Risky Code Lands
articles.content: Meta has moved Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) from research prototype into its production infrastructure . Meta JiTTests is an LLM-based system that writes executable tests designed to fail on a risky code change. A failing test is concrete evidence that a diff changed behavior. Meta team reports that JiTTests caught 74 privacy SEVs at the diff stage in the first half of 2026. The method is described in the FSE 2026 research paper ‘Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ‘. TL;DR Scale: Runs on Meta backend code with hundreds of millions of lines. The research paper analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Runs on: Meta’s internal infrastructure, overnight on spare capacity. Judge models in the paper: Llama3.3-70B, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4. Not publicly available. Performance: Engineers report a 60% true-positive rate at full scale (self-reported). Best: 74 privacy SEVs caught before landing in H1 2026; privacy SEV occurrence down 20%. Worst: The initial deployment confirmed only 8 of 41 reported catches (19.5%). Bottom line: Best: executable proof of a bug before merge. Worst: internal only, with self-reported numbers. What are Catching JiTTests? Catching JiTTests are LLM-generated tests that should fail when a diff introduces a bug. Traditional hardening tests pass when written and guard against future regressions. Catching tests target the change under review, before it lands. Meta formalized the details in its 2025 paper ‘Harden and Catch’ . Most AI bug tools act like faster human reviewers. They read the diff and leave comments. JiTTests instead execute code and show a concrete behavioral difference. Meta team concedes this takes more computational steps. It argues the approach catches bug classes that LLM or agent review can miss. How does the JiTTests pipeline work? The production pipeline has 5 stages: Targeting: Runs overnight on spare capacity. It selects the previous day’s risky diffs, using a mechanism similar to Meta’s Diff Risk Score. Test generation: 2 diff-aware workflows produce candidate tests (explained below). LLM-as-Judge ensemble: Several LLMs score each failing test using the test code, failure trace, diff and inferred intent. RubFake: The Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment adds deterministic checks. Its rules flag patterns like reflection, broken mocks and not-implemented exceptions. Human-on-the-loop: The system decides whether to contact an engineer, based on the combined ranking. Dodgy diff vs intent-aware: what is the difference? The dodgy diff workflow assumes every diff is buggy. It treats the diff as a mutant of its parent and generates tests that tell them apart. The intent-aware workflow first infers what the diff should do from its code, title and summary. It lists risks, builds a mutant for each, and writes tests to kill them. Tests that then fail on the real diff become ‘weak catches.’ What do the benchmarks show? The research team analyzes 22,126 generated tests. Diff-aware methods produced 4x more candidate catches than hardening tests. They produced 20x more than tests that failed by coincidence. The intent-aware workflow produced weak catches in 6.4% of its tests and on 7.9% of diffs. Dodgy diff scored 2.5% and 4.0%. Meta’s earlier ACH mutation-guided hardening scored 0.8% and 1.6%. The rule-based and LLM assessors cut human review load by 70%. articles.title: How Foreign Businesses Can Accept UPI Payments and Subscriptions in India
articles.content: A practical guide to market fit, local payment rails, recurring authorization, and the cross-border infrastructure behind a successful checkout India has one of the world’s largest digital audiences - and a payment environment that can punish assumptions imported from the United States or Europe. A checkout that supports international cards may technically accept a payment from India, but that does not mean it fits how a typical Indian customer prefers to pay. The opportunity is not simply to display prices in rupees. It is to choose the right rail, authorization experience, commercial partner, and renewal architecture. UPI deserves to be treated as a first-class option, not because cards are irrelevant, but because a card-only strategy can unnecessarily limit reach. Equally important: accepting a one-time UPI payment is not the same as making recurring UPI billing work for a foreign merchant. The distinction is where a large part of the engineering effort begins. 1. The scale of the market and what the numbers actually say India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) handled 241.62 billion transactions worth approximately ₹314.23 lakh crore in FY2025-26, according to a government release drawing on NPCI data. The number of transactions was around five times the FY2021-22 level. By June 2026, roughly 554.9 million users had been onboarded to UPI. These figures tell us that UPI has achieved extraordinary breadth; they do not, by themselves, prove its conversion rate for an online subscription checkout. UPI transaction totals span different use cases, including transfers between individuals and payments to merchants. Comparing every UPI transaction with only credit-card purchase transactions would be an apples-to-oranges comparison. The relevant question for a seller is narrower: how much of its own target audience can pay successfully, and how readily, with each method? That distinction matters. A foreign business does not need to replace cards completely. It should test whether adding UPI to a well-designed checkout increases payment completion among its intended Indian customers, without compromising subscription operations or compliance. 2. Why card-first checkouts create avoidable friction A credit card is a convenient default for many American subscription products. In India, it is a less universal starting point. Credit cards depend on issuer underwriting and access to a line of credit. RBI directions require issuers to assess an applicant's credit risk with reference to their independent financial means. Cards in circulation are also not the same as distinct people who hold an active, usable card. The problem is both availability and checkout readiness. RBI card-security rules require cards to be issued with domestic ATM and point-of-sale use enabled as the baseline, while cardholders can control online and international transaction settings. An Indian customer may have a card yet be unable to complete a cross-border, card-not-present transaction until they change issuer settings. That failure can look like an ordinary declined payment to the merchant. Preference also matters, but it deserves more careful language than a national stereotype. UPI’s familiarity, immediate account-based payment experience, wide merchant acceptance, and lack of a revolving credit requirement can make it appealing to customers who have access to both methods. Rather than assume all Indian consumers dislike credit, businesses should measure customer preferences, available instruments, authorization success and payment-method selection in their own funnel. Finally, payment behavior depends on context. An enterprise software buyer, a consumer news subscriber and a mobile-first video viewer may have very different card access, order values and tolerance for friction. The correct payment mix is a product decision informed by the segment, not a slogan that cards never work. 3. Pricing locally is a product decision, not an exchange-rate exercise The…

articles.title: Voice AI is quietly transforming frontline work
articles.content: It’s no secret that AI chatbots and agents are answering employee questions, writing code and emails, and taking on other tasks in office environments. But AI tools that communicate by voice, rather than through keyboards and screens, are also quietly taking off in frontline environments—from factory floors to retail stores. In some cases, AI that can understand spoken language is making it practical for workers to digitally access and share information in settings where protective gloves, outdoor weather conditions, or the need to operate other equipment have made traditional desktop or touchscreen devices difficult to use. “With the advent of AI, voice became possible as an interface,” says Peter Moeckel, founder and CEO of Frontier Audio . “And frontline workers—they’re using their hands, they’re using their eyes for the job. That’s why the touchscreen, the keyboard, or the mouse obviously doesn’t work.” [Photo: Frontier Audio] Frontier Audio, which has raised $4.5 million in pre-seed funding, offers audio hardware and software to connect workers in industries ranging from manufacturing to aviation, including through contracts with the U.S. Air Force. The company’s devices come in a variety of form factors, including over-the-ear headphones with noise cancellation and shoulder-mounted microphones, similar to the walkie-talkie-style equipment many workers already use to stay connected. The equipment lets users talk to colleagues or AI, helping with tasks like reporting maintenance issues before they cause production problems, locating equipment such as carts in sprawling facilities, and receiving important alerts without needing to stop and look at a screen. [Photo: Frontier Audio] “We cannot add extra work,” Moeckel says. “They already have an immense amount of work to do, and we need to get out of their way. And our platform, a big part of making it seamless and enabling easy adoption is it working just like a normal radio.” Frontier Audio is far from the only company building voice-powered AI for the workplace, often combined with radio services. Motorola Solutions offers AI features integrated into its police radios. Samsara, which builds connectivity and analytics tools for a variety of frontline operations, announced last month that voice commands have become the primary interface for people interacting with AI agents on its platform. Its voice bots can communicate with utility crews working on power lines, truck drivers arriving at unfamiliar worksites, and other workers in situations where they can’t look at a screen. MangoApps , which offers AI and intranet-style tools geared toward frontline workers, enables users to access information about scheduling, company policies, and other matters through either text-based chat or voice in their preferred language, typically from their existing phones. Andy Tolton, vice president of marketing at MangoApps, says many businesses realized during the COVID-19 pandemic that they had limited ways to stay in contact with employees outside of traditional office roles. “For the vast majority of businesses, their intranet is really a desktop paradigm,” he says. While workplace AI tools have often been built chiefly with office workers in mind, businesses are now realizing they can offer multilingual access to company data and processes to field employees who, in some cases, were still using clipboards and paper forms until recently. That’s thanks to improvements in audio processing that make speech recognition and freeform conversations less frustrating, even in noisy environments, alongside advances in the ability of AI models to deliver accurate information and take action on behalf of humans. “The speech AI technology has improved vastly, [as has] the knowledge that AI can access and be trained on,” Tolton says. “That, plus its ability to act, has increased exponentially in the last two to three years.” Still, as in office environments, rolling out…

articles.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
articles.content: This article is brought to you by VicOne . VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others. Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers. Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots. These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster , and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations . What AI changes about vulnerability discovery Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities. When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change. Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled. Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed. VicOne The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage. Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly. Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence. Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly. These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior. In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a…

articles.title: Alibaba Releases Qwen4-Max: 2.4T MoE, 71B Active, 1M Context
articles.content: Alibaba’s Qwen team has released Qwen4-Max , the first model of its Qwen4 generation. Qwen4-Max is a proprietary sparse MoE model with a 2.4T-parameter backbone and 71B parameters active per token. It accepts text, images and video, and supports a 1M-token context window . Alibaba also cut API prices and reports a 62% drop in average cost per task. TL;DR Size: 2.4T backbone parameters, 71B active per token, plus 328B N-gram Embedding parameters. 1M context, 393K max output tokens. Runs on: Hosted only: QwenCloud API, Token Plan, Qwen Studio, QwenWork and Qoder. No open weights, so no self-hosting or quantized builds. Performance: A large jump over Qwen3.8-Max. Competitive with frontier models on agentic work, behind on hard coding and vision. Best: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agent work): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1, the next-best model. What is Qwen4-Max? Qwen4-Max is a multimodal MoE language model from Alibaba, built for long-horizon professional work. A Token Plan-only preview opened this month only . How does the Qwen4-Max architecture work? Qwen4 upgrades the sparse MoE design in 3 places: attention, residual connections and embeddings. GDN + Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA): Each QSA layer pairs with 3 Gated DeltaNet layers. These compress history into fixed-size states. QSA then uses a lightweight indexer to pick relevant context at micro-block granularity. This lowers attention and indexing cost on long sequences. Gated Residual (GR): 4 parallel residual branches use dynamic read and write gates. The aim is stronger information flow and better training stability. N-gram Embedding: 328B extra parameters provide lookups of local token patterns at layer 2. This adds capacity with little extra compute. Alibaba reports no loss spikes across the 2.4T-scale pre-training run. On in-house tests, Qwen4-Max-Base shows 5 to 13% lower bits per byte than Qwen3.8-Max-Base. It does this while activating 25% fewer parameters. How does Qwen4-Max perform on benchmarks? Alibaba’s comparison chart covers 16 benchmarks. Rivals are Qwen3.8-Max-0902, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Kimi K3.1. Several scores are cited from third-party leaderboards. None were independently reproduced at launch. Qwen4-Max ranks first on 4 of 16 benchmarks: HLAB-Vals-1.1 (legal agents): 21.3, versus 11.7 for Kimi K3.1 and 9.2 for Opus 5.5. Agents’ Last Exam v1.1: 46.7, versus 43.4 for Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3.1. BioMysteryBench: 85.0, versus 84.4 for GPT-6.1 Sol. DeepSWE v1.1: 75.7, versus 75.5 for Kimi K3.1. Claude Opus 5.5 leads 7 of the 16 charts. Qwen4-Max trails most clearly on coding and vision: ProgramBench: 31.5 versus 65.0 for Opus 5.5. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 48.5 versus 67.2 for Kimi K3.1. Chartography: 54.2 versus 71.1 for GPT-6 Astra. Humanity’s Last Exam: 51.7 versus 59.8 for Opus 5.5. On Alibaba’s own Work360 benchmark, Qwen4-Max scores 52.69, up from 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Work360 spans 26 top-level domains and 721 specialized fields. Why is Qwen4-Max cheaper to run? Two things stack: fewer tokens and lower prices. On Work360, token use drops about 24% at Xhigh effort and 35% at High effort. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, the drops are about 48% and 49%. Average Work360 cost per task falls from $4.43 to $1.67, a 62% cut. List prices fell too. Input is $1.50 per million tokens , down from $2 for Qwen3.8-Max . Output is $4.50, down from $6. Implicit cache reads drop 70%, from $0.25 to $0.075. articles.title: Engineering Zero-State Search
articles.content: Open Spotify, Netflix, or almost any modern delivery app, and tap the search bar. Before you type a single letter, the screen is already full. You see recent genres, trending queries, categories tailored to the time of day, or items you lingered on yesterday. In information retrieval, this is the zero-state search. Traditional search engines are reactive. They wait for a text string, parse tokens, hit an inverted index or vector store, and rank candidates against explicit intent. zero-state search flips that sequence. The ranking decision happens before the user expresses any intent at all. That shift sounds like a minor UI convenience, but it changes the underlying systems problem. When you populate a search screen ahead of the first keystroke, you are trading explicit intent for latency and convenience. Get it right, and the user saves five seconds of typing. Get it wrong, and you have built a high-speed wall of stale, repetitive guesses that gets in the way of actual search. Here is how the engineering problem changes when ranking moves ahead of the query—and why standard offline relevance metrics usually fail to catch the worst UX bugs. The Precomputation Trap: Latency vs. Context When a user taps into a search bar, your latency budget is unforgiving. If zero-state suggestions take 400ms to pop in, the user has already started typing, and the UI jump when the suggestions finally render will cause mis-taps. To feel native, zero-state payloads need to resolve in under 50ms to 100ms—often served straight from a local device cache or an edge key-value store. Because you cannot run heavy multi-stage ranking at tap time, the work moves earlier. Candidate generation and scoring happen asynchronously: in nightly batch jobs, on app launch, or triggered by background event streams. Precomputation buys you speed, but it creates an immediate freshness problem. Suppose a user spends twenty minutes browsing hiking boots on an e-commerce app, buys a pair, and closes the app. If your zero-state pipeline relies on a batch job that recomputes user embeddings every six hours, the next time that user taps the search bar, your system will proudly suggest hiking boots. The prediction had a high offline probability score, but in the real world, the task is over. To make precomputed rankings work without feeling broken, teams usually have to split the scoring pipeline into two layers: The Slow Layer (Batch/Nearline): Computes broad affinity scores, collaborative filtering candidates, and long-term category preferences. This populates the candidate pool. The Fast Re-ranker (Edge/Client-side): Applies lightweight, deterministic rules at read time. It checks local session state, filters out items purchased or dismissed in the last ten minutes, and adjusts weights based on immediate context (like time of day or device connection). If you only build the slow layer, your app will feel like it has amnesia about what the user just did. Optimizing for Pointwise Relevance Breaks Discovery The most common mistake in zero-state ranking is reusing the exact same objective function used for standard search or home-feed click-through rate (CTR). When a user types "wireless mechanical keyboard", narrowing the results to ten nearly identical keyboards is a win. You have an explicit constraint. Before a query, you have no constraint. If your model notices a user clicked on Italian restaurants twice last week and responds by filling every slot on the zero-state screen with pasta places, you haven't built a discovery tool. You've built a rut. High pointwise scores do not equal a useful screen. If five candidates each have a 15% probability of being clicked, but all five represent the exact same intent cluster, showing all five wastes four slots. Instead of pure relevance sorting, zero-state ranking has to be treated as a portfolio optimization problem (or a slated recommendation problem). The goal isn't for every item on the screen to be right; the goal is for at…
