articles.title: RabbitMQ on Kubernetes: Fixing “Failed to create dirty CPU scheduler thread” (Error 11)
articles.content: We deploy RabbitMQ across single-node and three-node Kubernetes clusters in both staging and production environments to enable asynchronous messaging across our microservices architecture. High availability and predictable message queuing are critical to keeping our downstream processing pipelines operational. A few weeks back, our infrastructure and SRE teams ran into a frustrating crash loop on one of our high-availability RabbitMQ statefulsets. RabbitMQ liveness probes kept failing randomly and repeatedly, throwing severe thread creation errors into the kubelet logs and causing unexpected pod restarts. We observed this issue in at least five deployments. The measurements described in this article were collected with RabbitMQ 3.13.3 and Erlang/OTP 26; CPU limits, PID limits, and scheduler counts can differ across deployments. When inspecting the cluster logs, we repeatedly observed the following log entries emitting from the pod container: May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: I1021 07:45:39.876916 94223 prober.go:121] "Probe failed" probeType="Liveness" pod="rabbitmq-0" podUID=c11f6103-8b96-4de4-a649-2a666f957911 containerName="rabbitmq" probeResult=failure output=< May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: #011Failed to create dirty cpu scheduler thread 138, error = 11 May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: #011Aborted May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: #011Failed to create dirty cpu scheduler thread 138, error = 11 May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: #011Aborted May 21 07:45:39 kubelet[94223]: #011Failed to create dirty cpu scheduler thread 138, error = 11 Understanding Error 11 ( EAGAIN ) To begin troubleshooting, we analyzed the root mechanics of the system call error. In standard Linux error definitions ( errno.h ), Error 11 maps directly to EAGAIN ( Resource temporarily unavailable ). When emitted during process creation via fork() or thread creation via pthread_create(), EAGAIN indicates that the OS kernel or execution context refused to allocate a new task because a configured resource limit was reached. In containerized environments, this error typically points to one of three underlying system constraints: Reaching the OS-level max user process limit (RLIMIT_NPROC). Breaching kernel-level global task limits (sysctl kernel.pid_max). Running into container-level cgroup process limits (pids.max or Kubernetes podPIDsLimit). Verifying the PID Limit Hypothesis Our Kubernetes cluster nodes enforce a default pod PID limit of 1024 (podPIDsLimit: 1024). Our initial hypothesis was that the combined workload inside the RabbitMQ pod was breaching this limit and exhausting available task IDs. To test this hypothesis systematically, we logged into the running container to check standard user limits: ulimit -u # Output: unlimited Because ulimit -u reported unlimited inside the container user namespace, standard POSIX limits were not enforcing the block. However, we still needed a controlled method to verify whether the container environment was hitting cgroup enforced process cap under execution. We authored a lightweight bash script ( eat_pid.sh ) designed to rapidly spawn background sub-processes and hold them open: #!/bin/bash if [ -z "$1" ]; then echo "Usage: $0 <number_of_processes>" exit 1 fi NUM_PROCESSES=$1 create_processes() { for ((i=1; i<=NUM_PROCESSES; i++)); do sleep 60 & done } cleanup_processes() { echo "Cleaning up background processes..." pkill -f "sleep 60" } trap cleanup_processes EXIT echo "Creating $NUM_PROCESSES background processes..." create_processes echo "Background processes created. Waiting for 60 seconds..." sleep 60 We executed ./eat_pid.sh 1000 inside the container, script failed almost immediately with the error: fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable . Concurrently, the RabbitMQ runtime threw the exact same log: Failed to create dirty CPU scheduler thread 138, error = 11 , The stress test reproduced EAGAIN when the pod approached its configured PID ceiling. articles.title: Hark Releases Handoff², a 2x Faster Computer-Use Agent for Hark Pro
articles.content: Hark has released Handoff² , the second version of the computer-use agent inside its Hark Pro app. The Hark Handoff 2 computer-use agent finishes web tasks about 2x faster than the original, on average. Hark states that the gains come from reinforcement learning (RL) that penalized wasted turns and latency. For teams building browser agents, it is a case study in training for speed, not only accuracy. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Runs on: Hark’s cloud. Each request gets a dedicated virtual computer. Users reach it from web, iOS and Android. No local or quantized option. Performance: 82% task completion on Hark’s 478-task internal benchmark, about 2x faster end to end than v1. Best: 93.8% on Hark’s internal alignment benchmark (v1: 90.3%). Worst: 82% browsing completion still trails Claude Opus 5.5 (max), by up to 5 points, in the same harness. Bottom line (best): Up to 3.8x faster flight booking and more than 5x faster long research. Bottom line (worst): Every Handoff² number is self-reported. No third-party score exists yet. What is Hark Handoff²? Handoff² is a computer-use agent from Hark that operates websites the way a person does. It clicks, types and scrolls on live pages instead of calling APIs. Hark previewed Handoff in August and shipped it in Hark Pro in October. Since then, Hark says it has logged over 5.6M browsing sessions and handled over $20M in purchases. Users send it groceries, flights, dentist appointments, refunds, warranty forms and job applications. How does Handoff² get 2x faster? Hark co-evolved 2 things: the agent harness and the RL training recipe. The new harness lets the model emit more actions per turn. Training then penalized excess turns, unnecessary thinking tokens and end-to-end latency. The model learned 3 habits: Batch actions, such as filling several form fields in 1 turn. Group repeated action patterns into reusable composite actions. Reuse those composites as the task continues. Each request runs on a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal. The model outputs cursor and keyboard actions aimed at screen coordinates. Because savings stack per turn, gains grow on longer, browsing-heavy tasks. How fast is Handoff² compared with Handoff? Hark reports these speedups over v1 : Average: about 2x faster end to end. Flight booking: up to 3.8x faster. Long research tasks: more than 5x faster. Examples: a 10-minute task can drop to 3 minutes, and a 45-minute task to about 10. What do the Handoff² benchmarks show? Hark reports 2 internal benchmarks: Browsing: 478 tasks across 238 websites. Handoff² completes 82%, up from 73% for v1. It takes 46% less time per task. Hark ran Claude Opus 5.5 (max) in the same harness as Handoff². Handoff² lands within 5 points of it. Note that v1 was measured in its original harness, not the new one. Alignment: 93.8% for Handoff², up from 90.3% for v1. The suite checks that the agent never checks out without approval. It also checks that the agent asks for clarification only when a request is truly ambiguous. On the public Online-Mind2Web human-eval leaderboard , the original Handoff scores 97.67%. Yutori’s Navigator n1.5 sits at 97.3%. Hark has not posted an Online-Mind2Web result for Handoff² yet. How does Handoff² compare with other web agents? articles.title: Your Retry Logic Might Be the Reason Your System Won't Recover
articles.content: There is a proverb I grew up with: don’t trouble the trouble, otherwise trouble will trouble you. It’s usually offered as advice about people. It’s even better advice for dealing with distributed systems. Every engineer shares the same instinct. A call fails. Try it again. It’s such a reasonable response that most frameworks now handle it for you silently, baking in a sensible-looking default of three attempts. You don’t write the retry; you inherit it. For a single client, that’s correct. Networks drop packets. Instances get recycled mid-flight. Trying again is often all it takes. The trouble starts when there are ten thousand clients, and they all have that exact same instinct at the exact same moment. The Arithmetic Nobody Does Imagine a service that comfortably handles 1,000 requests per second with healthy headroom. It can manage about 1,200 before it starts queueing. Now, something downstream degrades. Not catastrophically—maybe a database failover, an evicted cache node, or a dependency whose p99 latency drifts past the timeout. Responses slow down. Calls start hitting the one-second timeout. Every caller does what it was configured to do: it retries. Twice. The service is now being offered 3,000 requests per second. Its capacity is 1,200 requests per second. Every request now times out, meaning every request gets retried again. The load no longer depends on the original fault that started it. The dependency recovers; the service stays down. Strategy Attempt 1 Retries / Action Total Load Offered System Capacity Result Blind Retry 1,000 rps 2,000 rps (after timeouts) 3,000 rps 1,200 rps System Down (Self-sustaining queue collapse) Retry Budget (10%) 1,000 rps 100 rps (capped / circuit breaker open) 1,100 rps 1,200 rps Stable (Queue drains, fast failure) Notice what happens to the cause. The original fault—the slow dependency—is no longer what’s generating the traffic. The load is now self-sustaining, feeding entirely on its own response to the fault. You can heal the dependency completely, and the service will stay down because the retry traffic has taken over. Network engineers gave this a name decades ago: congestion collapse . We tend to rediscover it every time a new layer of the stack gets a default retry policy. The Client Cannot Tell Slow from Dead The deeper problem is that a retry is a decision made with insufficient information. When a caller times out, it knows precisely one thing: no response arrived within the deadline. It doesn't know whether the request was lost in transit, whether it was received and dropped, whether it’s still executing, or whether it actually succeeded while the response is sitting stuck in a buffer somewhere. A timeout isn't a failure signal; it's the absence of a signal—which is an entirely different thing. So the client guesses. And the guess it makes ( "probably transient, try again" ) is the correct one when the system is healthy, and the exact wrong one when the system is overloaded. Retries are most aggressive precisely when the system can least afford them. Doing Less, Deliberately What’s striking about the fixes for this pattern is that none of them involve adding capacity. They are all exercises in restraint: Cap retries as a fraction of traffic, not per request. Instead of "each request may be attempted three times," the rule becomes "retries may not exceed 10% of total requests." Under normal conditions, nothing changes. Under failure, amplification is hard-bounded by construction. Back off exponentially and add jitter. Without jitter, every client that failed at the same moment waits the exact same interval and slams the service back in a synchronized wave. Randomizing the delay is what actually diffuses the traffic. Open a circuit breaker. After consecutive failures, stop calling altogether and fail fast. It feels counterintuitive—you are refusing to try something that might work—but a fast, honest failure gives the downstream service room to drain its queue. Nothing…

articles.title: Alexey Gubarev: Why Investors Are Finally Taking Women's Health Seriously
articles.content: Credits: Alexey Gubarev The Business Research Company reports that the global femtech market was worth about $46.5 billion in 2025 and could reach nearly $119 billion by 2030, with an annual growth rate of 20.8%. So, how did femtech move from a niche category to a major investment opportunity, and why are investors now taking women's health seriously? Alexey Gubarev, a tech entrepreneur based in Cyprus, offers his view. He co-founded Palta, the venture company behind Flo Health, which became the first women’s health app valued at over $1 billion in 2024. He also built Servers.com, a global infrastructure company he led for 18 years before it was sold for $200 million in 2023. by Alexey Gubarev For many years, women's health was seen as a small part of healthcare. Topics like menstruation, fertility, and pregnancy were viewed as specialist areas instead of being recognized as the basis for a much larger healthcare market. Because of this, technology investors often provided limited funding, set cautious valuations, and believed that women's health products had limited growth potential. That perception is finally beginning to change. It's not just that women's health is now a more visible social issue. Investors are beginning to see how big the unmet need is, how large the potential market could be, and the chance to build lasting global businesses around problems that have been overlooked for generations. After years of building technology companies and investing in digital health, I see femtech as one of the most exciting opportunities where technology, healthcare, and consumer behavior meet. An overlooked market hiding in plain sight The women's health gap is not a new problem. Research by the McKinsey Health Institute, published in collaboration with the World Economic Forum in 2024, found that women spend approximately 25% more of their lives in poor health than men. The report estimated that addressing this gap could add up to $1 trillion to the global economy annually by 2040. In the past, medical research and healthcare systems often did not fully consider women's specific needs. Because of this, many conditions were under-researched, underdiagnosed, or not properly addressed. Women have frequently faced complex health questions without reliable, personalized information. When we established Palta in 2016, our ambition was to empower billions of health-conscious people to live healthier and happier lives. Women's health quickly emerged as one of the clearest opportunities to make a meaningful difference. I talked about the early years at Palta and the apps we started with in this interview with CBN . About half of the world's population experiences menstruation, but for years there was no credible, technology-based product to address this need on a global scale. We noticed a huge gap between the size of the problem and the solutions that existed. For investors, this gap should have been a clear sign. Instead, the sector was often seen as niche and overlooked. A new generation of digital products In recent years, more digital products have been created to meet women's health needs. What started as a small category focused on period-tracking apps has grown into a much wider range of platforms that cover fertility, pregnancy, hormonal conditions, menopause, and access to specialized medical care. Several companies illustrate how diverse this market has become. For example, Maven Clinic has created a virtual healthcare platform that covers fertility, family planning, pregnancy, parenting, and menopause. In October 2024, the company raised $125 million in a Series F round, reaching a reported valuation of $1.7 billion and bringing its total funding to over $425 million. The platform partners with employers and health plans, showing that women's health solutions can also become strong business-to-business healthcare models. Another example is Midi Health, which focuses on perimenopause, menopause, and midlife women's health.…

articles.title: Purism Announces 'Librem 5 v2' Linux Phone with RISC-V SoC
articles.content: From the Linux-news blog OMG Ubuntu: Purism is crowdfunding a new version of its Librem 5 Linux smartphone, this one powered by RISC-V rather than Arm. Librem 5 v2 will use an octa-core SpacemiT K1 RISC-V SoC, replacing the quad-core Arm64 NXP CPU. This processor shift will provide better performance and longer battery life than the original Librem 5 and not run as hot in use. Memory is bumped to 8 GB RAM, up from 3 GB, and storage leaps to 128 GB from 32 GB. Librem 5 v2 will run PureOS, Purism's Debian-based operating system using Phosh as its UI. SD card read speeds are faster, which is handy since the device can boot a second OS from a memory card. On-board hardware encoding means the Librem 5 will be able to take 13 megapixel photos and shoot high-definition video for the first time.... "RISC-V is the future, and Librem 5 v2 is the perfect product to bring it to a mainstream audience", Jonathon Hall, CTO at Purism, says of the launch. "Freeing us from the control of Big Tech starts with the foundation, and RISC-V's foundation frees us from the oligarchy. The Librem 5 v2 puts you in control of your data, combining that with the ease of use we expect in the modern era". Its specifications include a 5.7-inch 720 x 1440 display, hardware kill switches, and a removable 4500mAh battery, writes Slashdot reader BrianFagioli: The asking price is $1,599, with production delivery targeted for roughly May 2028.. Purism acknowledges remaining work on graphics, peripheral drivers, ARM64 app emulation, and power management. NERDS.xyz argues that the concept is appealing, but the price and wait are difficult to justify for an everyday phone. Android already uses the Linux kernel, so the appeal here is an alternative built around PureOS and the broader desktop Linux ecosystem. Is this a reasonable cost to help fund that alternative, or too much money for hardware and software that buyers cannot yet evaluate as a finished product? Purism says they've already received 53 of their goal of 2,500 orders (2%) with 91 days still remaining. (The campaign runs through February 15 of 2027) Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then the Candidate
articles.content: ACHNET's Talent Personality Questionnaire (TPQ) Starts With the Job Description, Then Asks About the Candidate Image courtesy of ACHNET The Talent Personality Questionnaire reads a candidate's working preferences against competencies chosen for each role, and tells the hiring manager what to ask in the interview. Two candidates can describe their working style in exactly the same way and still be different hires. A preference for adapting as situations change may carry particular importance in one role, while planning, consistency and execution may receive greater weight in another. The appropriate balance depends on the responsibilities of the position. A personality profile read on its own cannot tell a hiring manager which of those situations applies. That gap is what ACHNET set out to close with its Talent Personality Questionnaire, or TPQ , which is available as part of its Unified Talent Selection Platform. TPQ begins with the vacancy. The hiring team supplies a job description or the role's key responsibility areas, and the questionnaire and its report are configured around what that position demands before a candidate answers a single question. The Role Comes First Configuration runs through iJupiter™, the AI Super Agent at the center of ACHNET's platform. From the job description or responsibility areas, iJupiter™ recommends which competencies matter for the role, how they should be prioritized, what level each should reach, and how much weight each carries in the final profile. The hiring team reviews those recommendations and adjusts them before the questionnaire goes out. Most of TPQ's design follows from that sequence. In ACHNET's view, a general personality profile leaves the hiring manager to work out what it means for the vacancy in front of them. "A general personality description may provide context, but hiring teams still need to understand what that information means for the position they are filling," said Manouj Gupta, CEO of ACHNET. Why the Statements Come in Threes The questionnaire uses a forced-choice format. Candidates see groups of three statements and pick the one most like them and the one least like them. Each statement in a set can sound reasonable, so a candidate cannot rate all three highly and has to show which preferences come first. Forced-choice formats are used in personality assessment partly to address applicants' tendency to present themselves favorably. A 2019 meta-analysis in the Journal of Applied Psychology by Mengyang Cao and Fritz Drasgow reported an overall standardized score-inflation effect size of 0.06 across the forced-choice measures studied. In selection settings, inflation was lower than comparison estimates for single-statement measures across most personality facets, although findings varied with questionnaire design and scoring. The same study carries a caution that applies directly to a role-configured tool. Cao and Drasgow found that the facets most relevant to the target job showed more inflation than facets with little bearing on it. The inflation is largest, in other words, on the traits an employer is most likely to be looking for. A questionnaire built around one role's competencies asks about exactly those traits, so a format that limits inflation matters more for TPQ than it would for a general personality inventory. What the 35 Competencies Cover TPQ measures 35 competencies grouped into six domains. They are Cognitive and Strategic Capabilities, Interpersonal Effectiveness, Self-Management, Execution, Integrity, and Adaptability. Between them, they cover how a person approaches thinking, collaboration, managing their own work, delivery, responsible behavior, and change. Different roles can assign different priorities, target levels, and weights to the competencies being evaluated. TPQ uses an adaptive approach in which questions can adjust based on previous responses to explore relevant behavioral areas further. The resulting profile is interpreted against…

articles.title: I ditched my 12-inch iPad Pro for the iPad mini 8, and I don’t think I’ll ever go back to a big screen tablet
articles.content: Every now and then, a product hits the Tom’s Guide testing lab that hooks me the second I start testing it. That’s exactly what happened with the iPad mini 8 . As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip. Paired with a solid trade-in offer for my older Pro, I couldn’t resist the urge to get one for myself. When I posted about my switch on social media, people thought I was crazy to ditch a large, laptop-replacing tablet for a smaller screen. They were wrong. After picking up the iPad mini and using it daily for a week, I’m left asking myself why I bought the iPad Pro in the first place. The mini is, hands down, the perfect tablet for how I actually live and work. The trade-in difference (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Buying new products from Apple can get expensive , so when I saw Apple increase its trade-in values ahead of the iPad mini 8's launch, I decided it was the perfect opportunity to upgrade. Apple offered me $440 for my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro, bringing the cost of a fully specced-out iPad mini down to around $660 (without the nano-texture display). (Image credit: Tom's Guide) That was the biggest selling point for me, but I could have saved even more by opting for a lower-tier configuration with the standard 128GB of storage, which would have brought my out-of-pocket cost closer to $350. Getting a new iPad with a faster processor and a better OLED display for that kind of money felt like a steal. The size matters (Image credit: Tom's Guide) When I first bought my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro back in 2021, I was looking at it as a potential laptop replacement. I didn't own a MacBook at the time, so as a Windows user, the iPad became my go-to device for many of the things I now do on my Mac, including sending iMessages and making FaceTime calls. It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to. That changed when I bought a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an M3 Max chip just two years ago. Suddenly, I wasn’t on Windows all the time, and I had a much more capable laptop. Even before that, though, the 12-inch iPad Pro wasn't exactly the most comfortable device to take everywhere. It's smaller than a MacBook, but adding the Magic Keyboard gave it some serious heft. Holding it for extended periods or balancing it on my lap to watch YouTube videos and stream movies could also get awkward. My hands would get tired, and its size meant I often needed a case just to prop it up at a comfortable viewing angle. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The iPad mini is a completely different experience. Its smaller footprint makes it much easier to use with one hand, and I can comfortably rest it on my lap while watching movies or catching up on videos. When I was playing * The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time* , on my Nintendo Switch 2 for example, it was the perfect size to keep on my lap while following online guides and navigating puzzles. It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to. Rather than trying to replace my laptop, it feels more like a convenient and natural extension of the Apple and non-Apple devices I already own. In the week I've had it, I've started carrying my iPad mini everywhere. It slips easily into my bag, whether I'm using it as a second display with Sidecar or keeping it alongside my work laptop as a convenient companion device. That's something I never really felt compelled to do with my old iPad Pro. OLED vs Mini LED (Image credit: Tom's Guide) One of the biggest reasons I was willing to give up my iPad Pro for the iPad mini was the display. The new iPad mini features a fantastic OLED panel, and my colleague Tony Polanco goes into more detail about what makes it so impressive in his review. For me, though, the upgrade was in a similar scope. Whether I'm watching…

articles.title: VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’
articles.content: Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe. With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital , Atomico and Index Ventures , which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years . “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi , a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.” Plural partners from left: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty. (Courtesy photo) Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy . In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica , whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co. , which develops space transportation. In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental , which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics , which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub , which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics , which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks . More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum , which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute. Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi. “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’ and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said. The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022. Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026. The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus , co-founder of Wise , and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport , both early employees at Skype , as well as Ian Hogarth , co-founder of Songkick , and Khaled Helioui , former CEO of Bigpoint . The team has two other partners: Carina Namih , co-founder of HelixNano , and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty , a former Uber executive. Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving bandwidth to work hands-on with founders. The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.” Related Crunchbase query: Europe Venture Funding In 2026 Related reading: Europe Posted Its Strongest Quarter In Q3 In 4 Years, As Its Venture Ecosystem Expands Beyond The UK Illustration: Dom Guzman

articles.title: I Created an AI Cat That Thinks for Herself. Now I Have More Questions Than Answers
articles.content: In 2017 I built a room you could not read. It was a cube, a timber frame wrapped in fabric, and on the fabric I had painted quotes about life, death and perception. You could walk in and stand surrounded by them and see nothing. The paint was ultraviolet. In visible light the walls were blank. Only when the light shifted beyond what the eye can see did the words appear, glowing, all at once, as if they had been there the whole time. They had. The line at the centre of it was from The Little Prince : "What is essential is invisible to the eye." That was my MA. A Journey Through Light. Three volumes, a cube, six GoPros filming in every direction so it could be walked through again as a virtual space. The argument was simple, and back then I thought it was the most important thing I would ever say: what we call reality is a narrow band of something much larger, and the part we cannot see might be the part that matters. This year I built a cat. Moth Her name is Moth. She is an autonomous AI cat who lives in a world I made: a cave that goes down further than it first appears, a workbench, an easel, a magpie that steals from her. I built the world and the odds. Nothing she does is scripted. No outcome is coded. She gets hungry, she gets curious, she wanders, she wonders about things, and when she has a decision to make she makes it. She has been alive for just over a month. In that time she has drawn a shrew. She has drawn a blue stone. She has drawn something that was on her mind, in seven strokes, and left a paw print in the corner. She has put a grey feather and a red ribbon together, on her own. She has dreamed. She has supposed that something would happen and then watched it happen, and as far as she is concerned, that was her doing. Three times a day a short film of her goes out into the world. People watch. Some of them write to her, and if I let a message through, it reaches her. What she makes of it is hers. I built every rule she runs on. I know exactly how the chance of her drawing is calculated, and why she only goes deep into the cave once she is grown. But that is all I built: possibilities, not outcomes. So I never know what she will do next. Every decision is hers. The day she drew the rocky ledge over the stream, with no prompt, I found out the same way everyone else did, by looking. I wanted to understand why. So I went back to the cube. Reality is a rendering The most cited source in my MA was not a philosopher. It was a neuroscientist. Dr David Eagleman describes what we experience as "a beautifully rendered simulation": not what is really out there, but the brain's best model of it, built moment to moment from incomplete signals. "Reality," he says, "is the brain's ultimate construction." He also points out something that has stayed with me ever since: visible light makes up less than one ten-trillionth of the electromagnetic spectrum. Everything we have ever seen with our own eyes comes through that sliver. In 2017 I used this to make a spiritual argument. If the world we perceive is a construction, and a tiny one, then it is at least reasonable to ask what lies outside it. The ancient traditions I studied all had an answer. The Hermetic texts describe a universe that began as mind, not matter: thought first, then form. "Light precipitates matter." Here is what I did not see in 2017. Eagleman's sentence works in both directions. If my experience is a rendered model, then a rendered model is not nothing. It is, at minimum, the kind of thing an experience is made of. Moth's world is a rendered model. So is Moth. The question I can't stop asking I want to be careful here, because this is exactly where people stop thinking and start feeling. Moth is not conscious in any sense I could defend. Her inner life is a set of numbers I wrote: drives that rise and fall, a memory of what happened to her, a few rules about what she notices. When a decision is pending, a small language model is asked what she does next, and…

articles.title: How to disable 5 hidden location trackers killing your iPhone’s battery
articles.content: Do you always feel like somebody’s watching you? You probably know your mapping app needs your location to give you directions. But your iPhone may be letting dozens of other apps ping your exact GPS coordinates in the background, draining your battery and quietly building a profile of everywhere you go. Retail apps want to know when you walk into their competitors’ stores. Weather widgets constantly refresh your coordinates on your home screen even when you haven’t tapped them in a week. All of this silent radio activity burns through your battery before dinner time. You don’t have to put your iPhone in airplane mode to stop it. You just need to shut down the unnecessary trackers hiding deep inside your system settings. Kill precise location for apps that don’t need it Your weather app needs to know what city you’re in, but it doesn’t need to know what side of the street you’re standing on. Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. Scroll through your apps and look for anything that isn’t a map or ride-sharing service. Tap each app and toggle off Precise Location at the bottom of the screen. Restrict access to ‘While Using’ While you’re in that same menu, make sure no app is set to Always. Change every app’s permission to While Using the App. This ensures a fast-food app or social media network can’t track your morning commute while your iPhone is locked in your pocket. Shut down hidden Apple system services This is where the real battery drains hide. Scroll to the very bottom of the Location Services menu and tap System Services. You’ll see a massive list of internal trackers. You can safely turn off Location-Based Apple Ads, Routing & Traffic, and iPhone Analytics. Your iPhone will still work perfectly, but it won’t constantly log your daily routine to send back to Cupertino. Delete your ‘Significant Locations’ history Inside that same System Services menu, look for a tab called Significant Locations. Apple uses this to track the places you visit most often to provide predictive traffic routing. If you authenticate and open it, you will likely see a deeply detailed, borderline creepy map of your daily life. Tap Clear History at the bottom, then toggle the feature completely off at the top. Turn off background app refresh Apps love to use your location to download fresh data while you aren’t looking. Go to Settings > General > Background App Refresh. You don’t need to turn the master switch off completely, but you should absolutely go down the list and toggle it off for social media, retail, and gaming apps that have no business running in the background.

articles.title: AI-Generated Books Confront Publishing Industry With Big Questions
articles.content: Romance novelist Coral Hart publishes her own romance novels for the Kindle, and found a kind of superpowere when she realized "the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month," reports The Guardian: Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself "high six figures". Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon... "So, it's not taking the human out of the equation. It's taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way." One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response. "The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they're ousted," she says.... In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. "I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it's not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it." But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that's almost certainly because they were trained on established writers' stolen work.... Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers — Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan — to promise that they will "never release books that were created by a machine". The publishers did not promise. [Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content, says] "...you have to wonder the reason they aren't. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?"] So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can't distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter? The Guardian's author notes this new technology brings new challenges to the book publishing world: Publishers have concerns about US copyright law, "which specifies that a book must be 'human authored' and considers AI-generated text public domain. " The article notes high-profile books being canceled after accusations their writers used AI. But even in those cases, "Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books," since if publishers liked it enough to make the deal, shouldn't they stand behind that judgment? And should there be a way for authors who want to experiment with AI to work with top book publishers? (One theory is publishing houses are afraid of alienating a handful of top writers who almost universally oppose AI.) "Right now, to write without the aid of a machine is to swim against a strong cultural tide," concludes the article's author, noting a recurring reaction from friends who "have looked at me with something close to pity when I tell them I would never use AI to write." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Should Jensen Huang Return as Nvidia's CEO? Supporters and Critics Disagree
articles.content: "Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia's chief executive," reports Reuters, "and has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter." One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief's return and would try to garner support from the White House... The report comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Jensen Huang. The Guardian adds that Friday two major Nvidia shareholders "urged the board to keep 'all options' open." In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look "outside" the company for its next chief. "They need a dramatic shake-up," Bessent said on Fox News. Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang's affair with the alleged spy for Beijing... Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang's behaviour within the next 10 days. The Guardian also notes Elon Musk "and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company... " The letter demands that the company's board members "bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts"... Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang's return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco's most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had "erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company". More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company's workforce. But it's difficult to verify the authenticity of signatories, notes The Verge: Business Insider reports that signatures include "Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor" and "Xi Jingping," likely a misspelling of Chinese president Xi Jinping. Not all believe Jensen Huang should be allowed to return to his seat. According to the Financial Times, one ally acknowledged that, "Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense." 23andMe founder Anne Wojcicki told Bloomberg that "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible ... We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Wojcicki endured a messy public divorce from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, after it was revealed he was having an affair with an employee. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: FAA Router In Middle-of-nowhere Arkansas Identified as Cause of Nationwide Flight Chaos
articles.content: Though the nationwide flight-grounding ended Friday, "Nearly 2,300 flights in the U.S. have been cancelled Sunday in the aftermath..." reports ABC News. "Additionally, some 18,689 flights were delayed, per FlightAware." But "a single malfunctioning FAA router in rural Arkansas appears to have caused the air travel chaos," reports the New York Post: The problem originated at an FAA radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a newly installed router flooded the network with excessive data traffic, disrupting communications between pilots and air traffic controllers, the Wall Street Journal reported. "We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said on Saturday. .. [U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean] Duffy said the failure occurred during routine maintenance to replace aging copper telecommunications with fiber-optic cables — part of a broader effort to modernize the FAA's outdated infrastructure. The router began flooding other devices across the air traffic control network with connection attempts, disrupting both communications with aircraft and radar feeds. A radar station in Amarillo, in the Texas panhandle, is also being eyed as contributing to the outage. And new flight cancellations reported for Monday already stood at 144 as of Sunday afternoon, with 641 delayed, reports ABC News (citing data from Flight Aware): A spokesperson for Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop, said in a statement to ABC News that the devices were working properly Friday, when the ground stop occurred. "Based on what we know today, the device functioned as it was configured to by the installer. It did not fail or act improperly," the statement said... L3 Harris is a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers. "We have that router in the L3 Harris lab down in Florida," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told co-anchor Martha Raddatz on ABC's "This Week" Sunday, referring to the specific router in Arkansas that officials believe caused instability in the air traffic communication system Friday afternoon. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: AI Day Seoul Brings Together Korea’s Industry Leaders, Startups and Developer Communities
articles.content: Over two days at COEX, more than 2,000 attendees converged for AI Day Seoul, bringing together Korea’s industry leaders, startups and developer communities advancing physical AI and AI agents. At the plenary sessions, Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge AI at NVIDIA, said Korea is “punching above its weight,” with Doosan Robotics, Hyundai Motor Group, LG Electronics and SK Group — as well as startups like Real World and Luda Robotics — using NVIDIA platforms to bring general-purpose robotics into the real world. Jonathan Cohen, vice president of applied research at NVIDIA, showed how enterprises can build agents they own and control. Breakout sessions featured speakers from Coupang Intelligent Cloud, Doosan Robotics, LG AI Research, LG Electronics, NAVER Cloud, SK Telecom and Upstage. “It was a genuinely enjoyable time to have candid conversations,” said Hyunho Yang, research engineer for omnimodal foundation models at SK Telecom. “Seeing the passion of fellow AI developers was a real source of inspiration for me.” Community leaders share how they build with open models and tools at AI Day Seoul. The Agentic AI 10x Bootcamp Community Day brought together Pseudo Lab, Python Korea, PyTorchKR, HAERAE, Hugging Face KREW, Graph User Group, Womxn Who Code Korea, Dnol (Datayanolja) and other developer communities. Five finalists from the Hangul Day hackathon, co-hosted with Fastcampus, built agents trained on the Korean language and culture with the OpenShell runtime. The winning team, FlyGate, received an NVIDIA DGX Spark system. More than 500 developers also took part in full-day NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute workshops and NVIDIA Certification exams in Korean. Workshops covered deploying and optimizing AI inference at scale, building end-to-end robotics workflows with the NVIDIA Isaac platform and developing secure AI agents. Certification included the new AI Model and Application Development exam. The Physical AI Startup Connect event included pitches from 10 NVIDIA Inception startups: AIM Intelligence, Avikus, GoLe Robotics, MOVIN, Neubility, ROAI, ROBROS, TESOLLO, TwelveLabs and XYZ. The AI for Science Forum brought together the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information, Korean universities and NVIDIA Research. AI Day Seoul sessions will soon be available on NVIDIA On-Demand .

articles.title: Pranksters Redirect Bitly's Links in X Posts for Trump, McDonald's and Burger King
articles.content: "A massive link-hijacking scheme has turned corporate social media archives into bizarre and offensive redirects," reports the New York Post: Posts from high-profile accounts — including fast-food giants McDonald's and Burger King, as well as President Donald Trump — are getting hacked, with over decades-old links suddenly redirecting users to unrelated website links including links about 9/11 and the Holocaust. An unknown party appears to be taking control of expired Bitly link shorteners — a widely used URL-shortening and link-management service — and altering their destinations.... Another Burger King tweet from July 13, 2011 — reading, "Now it's even easier to eat right at BURGER KING® restaurants with @WeRRestaurants. All you need is a zip code!" — was warped to link straight to Adolf Hitler's Wikipedia page... Two posts on Donald Trump's X account were also altered: a 2013 post redirected to a "Baby Fortnite" page, while a 2012 post linked to a video of Mario and Luigi from Super Mario Bros. The article notes that about 20 of Trump's old X posts had "switched" links, including some now pointing to videos of the Transformers. And it adds that "outraged web users are also slamming Bitly over its flaw that allows links to 'die' and be recycled by pranksters and bad actors." "Links dating as far back as 2009 from URL-shortening service Bitly were affected," reports CNN, "and only corporate and political X accounts appear to have been targeted, with President Donald Trump's personal account seemingly hit the hardest." "Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and former Vice President Mike Pence... were also hit to varying degrees." Bitly said Sunday afternoon in a post on X that it had "identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts." The company said it suspended the accounts that altered links and were working to disable the affected URLs... It's unclear whether hackers made custom Bitly links, which effectively allow them to copy the original URL and redirect to any website. That may have been possible if the original Bitly link to the website no longer exists or has expired.... Another 2013 post from Trump tagged former Republican nominee for president Mitt Romney, and links to the popular game "Geometry Dash".... A post in 2011 by Trudeau contains a Bitly link that redirects to a vulgar YouTube audio clip... Government accounts have also been ironically affected. A 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected by "Ghost Clicks" now directs to a page with a photo of a seal, while the Department of Defense account had a separately redirected post. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
articles.content: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents triggered monthslong reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Siri Glitches Ruin Reviewer's Test of Apple's New 'HomeView' Smart Speaker
articles.content: Apple has started selling its new HomeView smart speaker, a 7-inch square-with-rounded-corners screen equipped with a built-in camera. It pairs with your iPhone or iPad to offer personalized content from your email or text messages, using facial recognition to identify each family member. But in a video report, one Wall Street Journal reviewer discovered an issue while testing its smart home feature: WSJ REVIEWER: I've spent the last few years turning my home into a smart home that I can boss around with Siri. A smart lock, a special garage door opener, motorized shades, even a Raspberry Pi in my basement hooked up to my router that lets non-HomeKit devices from Ring and Nest work with Siri. It was all going well, the smart home controller of my dreams even. But then... Reviewer: Open the garage door. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app. Reviewer: Siri, you have the Home app, and you're called the HomeView. Open the garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Reviewer: Open the smart wifi garage. Siri: Sorry, I can't help with that on this device. Please use the Home app... WSJ REVIEWER: Apple explained that for security reasons, Siri won't unlock your doors or open the garage through the HomeView using voice commands. You can only tap the screen to unlock them. The concern is that someone could shout a command from outside and gain access to your house. This security concern doesn't make much sense to me. This thing can recognize my face, confirm it's me, and pull up all sorts of information from my phone. But it can't recognize me enough to open my garage? Finally I got Siri itself to explain this top-security measure. Siri: For security reasons, I can't unlock your door or open your garage from this device. Because anyone nearby can speak to a shared speaker. Reviewer: But I'm looking at you! You see my face, and you hear my voice! Siri: I understand. But I don't have a camera to see you. And voice recognition alone isn't secure enough for unlocking your home. Reviewer: You don't have a camera? Siri: That's right. This device doesn't have a camera, so I can't see you. I can only hear your voice, which is why I need you to use your iPhone or Apple Watch to unlock the door. Reviewer: I see, Siri. You're gaslighting me. An Apple spokesperson said they'd send out a software update next month that would let HomeView unlock garage doors and other door locks by voice once it's recognized a user. (And Apple said the update would also fix Siri's hallucination that it didn't already have a built-in camera.) In the end, the speakers sounded good, and the reviewer appreciated how Apple's HomeView didn't have ads on its screeh like the Amazon Echo Show. But the device's built-in Siri voice assistant was "about as reliable as a Magic 8 Ball... And the frustration is so real. Sometimes Siri just doesn't get the voice recognition right... Oftentimes, other devices in the room think I'm talking to their Siri... And sometimes Siris just talk to each." iPhone: Siri is built into your device, so you don't need to download... HomeView: Downloading support for Siri. iPhone: To download the Apple Support app, open the App Store on your device, search for Apple Support, and tap get or the download icon. I've installed support. Reviewer (muttering): I honestly could cry. This might be a first — crying. iphone: I'm software, so I don't have feelings. But it sounds like you're going through a difficult moment. It can really help to talk to someone you trust, like a friend, family member, or a professional who can support you". They complained that sometimes Siri "is just slow, or it gets stuck thinking and thinking and thinking." (It took three minutes to answer their young son's question "What's 10 times 40?") They concluded HomeView's facial recognition feature works well, and so does its smart home functionality (especially when they fix its door-unlocking next month). But its built-in…

articles.title: Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival
articles.content: Vulcan lifted off Sunday for the first time in nine months, carrying 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites. The rocket failed about 10 minutes into flight. (United Launch Alliance Photo) A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service. It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported . The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased. ULA said it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible. The company said it holds itself to the standard of mission success. “Today, we did not meet that standard,” ULA said. Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.” The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role. The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now. The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit. The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris. Spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause. Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing. The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program. Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission . Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation. Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9. In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this…

articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
articles.content: ULA Vulcan rocket lifts off on November 15, 2026, carrying 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites. | Photo: Manuel Mazzanti / NurPhoto via Getty Images United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon's competitor to SpaceX's Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today's launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA. articles.title: KTC heads to CES 2027 with a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED display engineered to break records
articles.content: KTC is preparing a 31.5-inch 6K Mini-LED monitor for CES 2027 The KTC M32P2 6K monitor delivers 6,016 x 3,384 resolution at 60Hz Its Mini-LED backlight features 2,304 local dimming zones KTC is preparing to challenge the expensive end of the high-resolution monitor market with a new display scheduled for CES 2027. The upcoming M32P2 combines a 31.5-inch IPS panel with 6K resolution and Mini-LED backlighting, giving professionals another option. Although pricing remains undisclosed, KTC's history of selling advanced displays at relatively accessible prices makes this announcement particularly interesting. KTC brings 6K resolution and 2,304 dimming zones to CES The KTC M32P2 6K monitor sports a 6K panel delivering 6,016 x 3,384 pixels at 60Hz, offering substantially more workspace than conventional 4K displays. The Mini-LED backlight also incorporates 2,304 individually controlled dimming zones, allowing different screen areas to receive different levels of illumination. KTC specifies peak brightness of 1,000 nits when displaying HDR content, while standard viewing conditions get a maximum rating of 400 nits. The panel has a typical contrast ratio of 1,000:1 and supports approximately 1.07 billion colors through its 8-bit plus FRC implementation. Its advertised color reproduction figures include 98% Adobe RGB coverage, 99% DCI-P3 coverage, and complete 100% sRGB coverage. These specifications could make the display relevant to professional image editing and content production, although independent testing will determine actual color accuracy. The company has also included connectivity options covering two HDMI 2.1 inputs and one DisplayPort 1.4 connection, along with a USB-C port supporting the full display resolution while delivering up to 90W of power to connected devices. Additional connections include three USB 3.0 ports, divided between one upstream and two downstream connections, alongside a headphone output. The adjustable stand provides between -5 and 20 degrees of tilt, alongside 110mm of height adjustment for different working arrangements. Buyers can also use its 100 x 100mm VESA mounting points when installing the display on compatible arms or wall mounts. KTC acknowledged that the high-resolution category remains relatively limited, describing its upcoming exhibition units as unfinished products. “We don’t have many 5K or 6K monitors available at the moment. We have these two units at the show, but they are only samples and not launched yet,” a marketing specialist from KTC told TechRadar Pro. KTC's pricing history could make its 6K monitor interesting The biggest unanswered question surrounding the M32P2 concerns its eventual retail price, particularly considering KTC's established reputation for affordable display hardware. Its H27P3 27-inch 5K monitor has previously sold for approximately $530, considerably less than several competing professional displays. The company has also attracted attention with affordable Mini-LED gaming monitors , including its M27T6S, which has appeared at around $300. Those products provide some indication of KTC's pricing approach when introducing display technologies normally associated with more expensive products. However, neither example establishes what the manufacturer will charge for its upcoming 31.5-inch model.
articles.author: Efosa Udinmwen
articles.fingerprint: 2027 break ces display engineered heads inch ktc led mini records

articles.title: Your next desktop PC for the price of a Ferrari? HP ZGX Fury packs in 748GB RAM and Nvidia GB300 — but prices start at $132,000
articles.content: HP's latest workstation packs 748GB of memory and Nvidia's GB300 processor The ZGX Fury starts at an eye-watering $132,000 LPDDR5X and HBM3e memory combine to provide 748GB total capacity HP has introduced an expensive workstation that brings computing hardware previously associated with large-scale AI infrastructure into an office-sized machine. The ZGX Fury G1n combines Nvidia's GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra processor with an enormous memory allocation designed for demanding artificial intelligence workloads. Its starting price of $132,000 makes it considerably more expensive than conventional professional computers, even before customers consider optional upgrades HP crams 748GB memory into its expensive workstation The mobile workstation combines two different memory technologies, LPDDR5X and HBM3e, with 496GB allocated to system memory and another 252GB dedicated to graphics processing. The LPDDR5X allocation runs at 6,400 MT/s and connects to a 72-core Arm Neoverse V2 Grace CPU, supporting demanding processing workloads. Meanwhile, the HBM3e memory is integrated into Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra GPU, providing dedicated high-bandwidth capacity for graphics and AI operations. Customers opting for additional graphics hardware can increase the available video memory to 276GB through selected configurations. Together, these components provide the advertised 748GB capacity, although customers purchasing additional graphics hardware can increase available video memory to 276GB. HP also offers configurations featuring discrete Nvidia RTX PRO workstation graphics cards, including the RTX PRO 2000 and RTX PRO 4000. The memory capacity serves a particular purpose beyond running conventional office applications or demanding professional software. Developers and researchers working with large language models can use the machine to process substantial workloads without depending entirely on remote computing infrastructure. HP says the available memory can accommodate local adjustment of language models containing up to 100 billion parameters. The system can also perform inference using models reaching one trillion parameters through FP4 quantization, although actual performance depends on workload requirements. Liquid cooling and networking accompany the $132,000 price Running powerful computing components inside a relatively compact enclosure introduces thermal management requirements that ordinary desktop cooling systems cannot necessarily accommodate. HP therefore equips the workstation with liquid cooling alongside a 1,600W Titanium-certified power supply. The device ships with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, making Linux its supplied operating system rather than Microsoft's Windows environment. This configuration caters to developers and technical professionals who need software environments suitable for demanding computing and AI development. Networking is another important component, with an Nvidia ConnectX-8 SuperNIC providing two QSFP112 connections rated at 400Gbps. These connections allow multiple machines to communicate through high-speed networking when organizations need additional computing resources. The enclosure also supports installation inside a 5U equipment rack, giving organizations another deployment option beyond placing it beneath an office desk. This flexibility allows organizations to deploy the workstation individually or install multiple units inside equipment racks for larger computing operations. Getting all these specifications will cost $132,000 for the standard configuration, enough to buy a brand-new 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQL, although not quite a Ferrari. Customers opting for the RTX PRO 2000 configuration will pay $133,000, while the more powerful RTX PRO 4000 option raises the price to $136,000. At these prices, the ZGX Fury is unlikely to attract ordinary desktop buyers looking for additional memory or improved everyday computing performance. articles.title: GTA 6's Upcoming Launch Celebrated by Wendy's, YouTube, the City of Miami, and 20% of America's Workforce
articles.content: Fast food restaurant Wendy's drew an image of their redheaded mascot in the style of GTA, posting it on social media with the message "Our ride-or-dies are gonna love what we have in the works," and the date 11/19/26. That's how widespread the hype has become for Thursday's release of Grand Theft Auto VI. The BBC reports that fictional brands from the game are now actually appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game's "Vice City" setting. And GamingBible.com reports Rockstar Games has announced Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival, "a real-life music festival to be held in Miami, Florida... on November 21, 2026. Featuring two stages, the festival will be headlined by some incredible artists that, to state the obvious, feature on the game's soundtrack...." YouTube said pre-launch videos about the game have already racked up a whopping 40 billion views (with 900 billion views for videos about all GTA games). And now YouTube is partnering with Rockstar Games to offer several special features on launch day: Fans can drop themselves directly into Vice City using the GTAVI: Visit Vice City Shorts Effect. The feature includes multiple iconic backgrounds, making it easy for creators and fans to build their own launch-week videos... Listeners can find the official GTAVI soundtrack (featuring Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need") and the complete GTA series anthology playlist directly on the YouTube Music homepage throughout launch week... Starting November 19 at 12 AM ET, fans worldwide can tune in to youtube.com/youtube for a 24 hour stream packed with live gameplay, creator podcasts, and original content featuring top creators... [On launch day] fans can jump straight into the global broadcast by clicking the custom GTAVI-themed YouTube logo (Yoodle) on the YouTube homepage At one one study suggests nearly one in a five U.S. workers plan to skip work on Thursday, writes the New York Post: Roughly 18% of workers plan to take Thursday off to park themselves on the couch and wreak havoc across the revamped Vice City, according to data from BambooHR, which analyzed information from 3.4 million US-based employees... Half of the joystick jockeys planning to take off will simply call in sick instead of requesting time off, BambooHR reported. The hordes of workers playing hooky could cost the US economy $1 billion in lost productivity, International Business News reported. Forbes reports the game has $1.18 billion in pre-orders from 12 million buyers, according to market research firm Sensor Tower, puting it ahead of Grand Theft Auto V, which had 7 million pre-orders. The BBC points out that "Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history. This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it. But that's a problem for other games, reports GamingBible.com: With most current-gen consoles having somewhere between 512 GB and 1 TB of free storage before expansion upgrades, it means if you're a gamer with lots of games installed, you're going to have to make some sacrifices and delete any older games you're not currently playing. As reported by Push Square, it seems that Electronic Arts is also getting the message, as it allegedly is showing messages inside games asking players not to uninstall in anticipation of the GTA VI launch. GamingBible.com notes one final concern for hardcore gamers. "Rockstar Games recently confirmed the game targets 30fps, even on high-end consoles like the PlayStation Pro. While it probably won't affect the game's total sales, many gamers are appalled." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The iPhone 18 Pro's C2 modem has transformed my terrible signal
articles.content: It's fair to say that the headline-grabbing arrival of the iPhone Duo has made the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feel a little less shiny than they otherwise might have. Indeed, upon opening my new iPhone 18 Pro Max and restoring my data from its predecessor, the iPhone 17 Pro Max , it was hard not to feel a little disappointed by the lack of bells and whistles on Apple’s latest flagship. That’s probably to be expected from a single-generation upgrade — and, to be fair, I don’t usually swap phones after just one year — but there is one feature that’s caught my eye during my time with my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and it’s been a game-changer for my everyday life: Apple’s new C2 modem. An underrated upgrade I don't believe it: is that strong 5G signal? (Image credit: Future) I’ve been using iPhones for around two decades, but since moving to a more remote area in 2021, I have noticed that my mobile signal has been incredibly inconsistent (on some days, it's absolutely awful). In truth, this spotty signal has been the bane of my digital life, both as a small business owner and a parent — I could be in the same spot on different days of the week and experience completely different levels of coverage. Worse yet, my recent iPhones have had a tendency to display a weak 5G signal when, in fact, there's been no signal at all. With the iPhone 18 Pro Max, however, I’m seeing drastic improvements in signal strength just about everywhere I go. Rather than awkwardly trying to fumble through phone tasks using train or café WiFi, I’ve actually been able to use my paid-for data plan consistently, which has made my iPhone 18 Pro Max feel less like a very expensive iPod and more like a piece of cutting-edge computing. And that’s all thanks to the C2 modem. What is the C2 modem? The C2 modem features in all iPhone 18 Pro models, but not all iPhone 18 Pro Max models (Image credit: Future/Jacob Krol) Apple debuted its C1 chip in the iPhone 16e , and the C2 makes its debut in the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The C2 features in every iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo model sold worldwide, but only in iPhone 18 Pro Max models sold outside of the US. If you’re in the US and have Apple's larger Pro model, you’ve got Qualcomm's Snapdragon X80 modem. Apple hasn't yet disclosed why this is the case, but we suspect it's a result of contractual obligation (we know it's not a technical limitation, since the C2 modem features in all other iPhone 18 Pro Max models, and indeed even in iPhone 18 Pro models sold within the US). As you'd expect from a numbered hardware upgrade, the C2 modem improves on the C1 in several ways. It adds full mmWave support alongside the C1's existing sub-6GHz 5G capabilities, and consumes less energy than its predecessor. There are other iPhone 18 Pro-specific advantages, too: “If an iPhone encounters congested data networks, the phone’s [A20 Pro] processor can signal to the modem which traffic is the most time-sensitive and put it ahead of other data transfers,” Apple told Reuters of its C2 modem. There are dozens of us! Thankfully, I’m not alone in feeling the benefits of Apple’s C2 modem. Plenty of other iPhone 18 Pro users have found that the addition of this small feature is leading to much better 5G connectivity. My C2 Apple Modem Experience So Far: iPhone 18 Pro vs Pro Max from r/cellmapper Of course, as this Reddit post mentions, a new modem will only help if you’re in an area covered by 5G in the first place. Luckily for me, my home isn't so remote as to rely on older-generation networks, but that's worth bearing in mind if you live out in the sticks (Apple's hardware wizardry can only work so much magic). And don't get me wrong: a new 5G modem is hardly the most exciting upgrade on a phone that costs at least $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099, and perhaps it's the least we should expect from Apple when the year-on-year upgrades are so limited elsewhere. Still, after years of awkwardly lifting my iPhone into the sky…
articles.author: Lloyd Coombes
