articles.title: Nvidia engineer leaves company over lack of transparency around Jensen Huang’s exit, details decision
articles.content: Just days after Jensen Huang suddenly resigned from his position at Nvidia , an Nvidia Robot Research Engineer said that he would leave the company as well. But more than just showing support for the former CEO with a generic “I stand with Jensen” message, Darrel Dai laid out several reasons for the decision on X . I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.That is why this has been so disappointing.I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.These are my personal views. November 15, 2026 “What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me,” the engineer posted. “I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.” It seems that Jensen Huang has gained the respect of the people working under him, with many calling for his reinstatement despite the many controversies he is currently facing. There’s also an online petition demanding that the Nvidia board “Bring Jensen Back,” with over 150,000 signatures at the time of writing. Nvidia is centered around Jensen Huang, with the former chief executive reportedly having a small army of 60 people directly reporting to him. But despite his busy schedule and legendary persona, Dai said that “Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly,” and that “It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.” Dai also pointed out that “employees’ trust and sense of belonging” are part of what makes a company great. articles.title: Apple's Smart Glasses Strategy Hinges on Siri and iPhone Apps
articles.content: Apple plans to unveil its first smart glasses at WWDC in June 2027 and begin shipping them before the end of the year, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman . In the latest edition of his "Power On" newsletter , Gurman shared new details about the glasses' design, charging system, and Siri features. Current prototypes of the glasses, internally code-named "N50," are reportedly slightly thinner than Meta's second-generation Ray-Bans. Some test units have oval camera openings integrated into the frame without protruding housings. A front light indicates use or charging, while Apple is experimenting with additional privacy features. Apple is apparently developing multiple styles and colors, with an emphasis on materials, sensors, and audio quality. Employees have described the sound as "industry-leading," with the glasses supporting music playback, calls, and FaceTime audio. Testers can also charge the prototype glasses while wearing them. A flat, three-pin magnetic connector, "roughly the size of a Tic Tac," attaches near the end of the left temple arm. Gurman said it remains unclear whether Apple will use this charging system in the shipping product. The first model will not display augmented reality imagery. Wearers will interact through ‌Siri‌, which will use the cameras to answer questions about their surroundings. Planned uses include identifying buildings, suggesting meals based on ingredients in a refrigerator, providing directions, and translating signs and conversations. Apple also intends to support calls, messages, iPhone notifications, calendars, standard and visual reminders, music controls, and smart home controls. To support the glasses, developers will need to let ‌Siri‌ control specific features in their iPhone apps. Apple envisions tasks such as booking restaurant tables, requesting rides, ordering coffee, shopping, and purchasing movie tickets working on the device. Developers will not need to create separate apps for the glasses. Their software will run on a paired iPhone, with the two devices working together to fulfill requests. Current plans require a recent iPhone model, with no Android support. The paired phone will compensate for the glasses' limited processing power and memory. Wi-Fi will allow certain functions outside third-party apps to remain available without a nearby iPhone. Gurman suggested audio playback could theoretically continue over Wi-Fi, although the glasses will not function as a fully independent device. Internal prototypes purportedly run a reduced version of visionOS 28 and contain a processor derived from older Apple Watch chips. Other custom components handle wireless connectivity and process images as the cameras capture them. Apple began introducing the necessary ‌Siri‌ controls in this month's first iOS 27.3 beta, enabling more precise control of app actions. Originally demonstrated in 2024, the capability has been rebuilt using newer AI models. Apple plans to release support for its own apps in December, followed by third-party support in 2027. Apple wants developers to prepare those integrations before the glasses arrive and continues to target a WWDC announcement next year. The company sees access to its existing app ecosystem as a major selling point against rival smart glasses. The device will also overlap with camera-equipped AirPods, which remain scheduled for launch in late 2027 and will also provide ‌Siri‌ with information about the user's surroundings. The glasses should offer longer battery life and accommodate more sensors, with Apple seeing the potential for them to be worn throughout the day. Work on the glasses started in the early 2020s, and Apple is said to have largely settled on the hardware. The remaining obstacles involve software and AI, which Gurman said are running late and could delay the planned 2027 launch. articles.title: Huawei Set To Challenge Tesla Powerwall with New, 20 kW Home Battery
articles.content: "Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery," reports Electrek: This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla's latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark... The Chinese tech firm is calling it an "all-in-one residential energy system" that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that's available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW. The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei's proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It's so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes. Huawei's basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with "just" 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. That's enough to keep essential household appliances, lighting, and electronics running during a power outage, but you'll want to keep going if you're preparing for more than a day or two without power. If that sounds like you, Luterra's got you covered. The modular system can be expanded with modular 7 kWh LFP battery packs and can keep scaling up to a massive 336 kWh of total storage across interconnected systems, with inverter output peaking at an impressive 60 kW using three 20 kW units in parallel. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Cockpit-Simulator 737X CDU (v2) Review: An Essential Component for Flight Sim Enthusiasts
articles.content: Thanks to the popularity of Microsoft Flight Simulator 2020, followed by Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, a growing number of companies have entered the flight simulation peripheral market — offering everything from budget-friendly products to high-end equipment designed for professional and home cockpits. Cockpit-Master and Cockpit-Simulator were jointly founded in 2018 to develop and manufacture flight simulation equipment. In 2024, the company was split into two divisions, with Cockpit-Simulator focusing on more premium, professional-grade equipment. Today, we are looking at the CS 737X CDU v2, a 1:1 replica of the Boeing 737 Control Display Unit (CDU). We will examine its build quality, how closely it replicates the real 737 CDU, and how well it integrates with Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024. The Real Boeing 737 Control Display Unit Before taking a look at the product itself, let’s first look at the real 737 Control Display Unit (CDU) and explain its functionality. The CDU is the primary interface pilots use to interact with the aircraft’s Flight Management System (FMS). The FMS can be thought of as the aircraft’s “brain,” handling a wide range of navigation and performance-related tasks. Pilots use the CDU to enter and modify the flight plan, while the FMS calculates the lateral route and vertical profile of the flight. It also manages performance calculations, monitors fuel and flight progress, and provides guidance to the autopilot. (Image credit: flaps2approach.com) The CDU features a display screen with six line select keys on either side. These keys allow pilots to select and enter information into specific fields on the display, including data entered into the scratchpad. The CDU also includes dedicated function keys for tasks such as accessing performance information and entering instrument departures and approaches. Below the display is an alphanumeric keypad, which pilots use to enter text and other data before transferring it to the selected field using the line select keys. Build Quality Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Unlike other consumer grade CDUs on the market, the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a full-metal, CNC-machined aluminum shell. The buttons are made of silicone rubber, which also closely replicates what we felt in our time on a 737 simulator. The display is where we noticed the biggest departure from the real 737 CDU. The real unit uses a thick, chemically strengthened, anti-glare optical glass cover, whereas the CS 737X CDU v2 uses a standard commercial display. As a result, there is some glare, although the display itself is excellent and offers very wide viewing angles. Despite this difference, the visual presentation is remarkably close to that of the real 737 CDU. The font styling, image sharpness, and color reproduction all closely match what you would see on the real flight deck. The CS 737X CDU v2 also features a handle, which on the real aircraft is used for the maintenance crew to remove the CDU. This isn’t entirely necessary in a home setup, but it is a nice touch. The unit can be easily placed on a desk using the included desktop stand, or integrated directly into a larger cockpit setup. The Feel (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) The weight, rigidity, and metallic construction closely replicate the feel of the CDU we experienced in a 737 simulator. The silicone buttons also require a firm, deliberate press to actuate, helping prevent accidental double-inputs during turbulence. This tactile resistance closely matches the experience of using the real unit. Manually entering a long route, rather than importing it from SimBrief, will give your fingers a workout – and will give you a newfound appreciation for the import button. articles.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 stock returns to Newegg with 21 models
articles.content: After rumors of Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 graphics cards being withdrawn from the consumer retail channel, it is pleasing to see major U.S. e-tailers like Newegg stuffed with stock today. Checking out this popular online electronics retailer, we note that there are 21 RTX 5090 SKUs available , and 11 are sold by and shipped by Newegg. Sadly, pricing remains in 3x MSRP+ territory at the time of writing. Remember, you can sift through pricing trends in our comprehensive GPU price tracking 2026 feature to see that Nvidia's Blackwell flagship was once available at its fabled sub-$2,000 price. (Image credit: Newegg ) Despite what looks on the surface like an ample supply (but there are order limits of one per customer), prices for RTX 5090s remain extremely high. The best prices we can see at Newegg are $6,599, but this price applies only to a water-cooled Aorus model and another sold inside a Gigabyte AI BOX eGPU . They might still appeal to you, depending on your setup, though. For a ‘standard’ air-cooled graphics card, albeit a very nice Aorus RTX 5090 Master , you’ll need to squeeze at least $6,659 out of your savings. A bonus with this card, alongside several others from the Gigabyte stables now purchasable from Newegg, is that it comes with a free motherboard. Many of these Gigabyte Aorus designs are being bundled with a full-ATX-sized X870 Aorus Elite WIFI7 AM5 motherboard , purportedly worth $319. Please note that the same motherboard is available to purchase outside this bundle for a more reasonable $249. If you have money to burn, there are plenty of even more expensive SKUs to pick from. There are no opulent Golden Dhabab models on Newegg, sadly, but you’ll still be asked to part with $11,896 for the Asus ROG Astral GeForce RTX 5090 Edition 20 (sold by a Newegg marketplace partner). Perhaps surprisingly, given recent trending pricing news, that’s the only model above $10K, but there are still many models that are almost $10,000 from Asus, MSI, and Zotac. Even an Nvidia Founders Edition RTX 5090 refurb is priced at $8,899. In context, these RTX 5090s are still at astronomical prices for consumer gaming PC add-in hardware. But they are now purchasable from a big retailer with fast delivery, rather than off a random scalper. It was only a month ago that rumors swirled about the RTX 5090 and the RTX 5080 being withdrawn from retail. articles.title: Bill Gates Has Earned Billions Investing in Climate-Polluting Landfills, Reports ProPublica
articles.content: Environmental activist Bill Gates has "quietly accumulated a $29 billion stake in America's No. 2 landfill operator, Republic Services," reports ProPublica, in a new 5,000-word investigation. But inspectors from America's Environmental Protection Agency "have repeatedly found methane — a highly potent greenhouse gas — escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. Republic has lobbied against regulations that could make the waste industry cleaner, including by keeping organic garbage out of landfills in the first place." While Gates has invested at least $2 billion in green companies, he's "put more than double that amount into a very dirty, old-school industry," their article argues. And Gates has increased his stake in Republic "to 38% of the company, a position worth $29 billion." While fossil fuels get most of the attention, scientists increasingly see landfills as a crucial climate issue. They're responsible for as much as a fifth of the country's emissions of methane, a highly potent greenhouse gas, studies show. Republic alone generates as much climate pollution as 3 million gasoline-burning cars each year, according to its own reports.... [Gates] has failed to make Republic live up to his own climate principles, a ProPublica investigation has found. Federal inspectors have repeatedly found methane escaping from Republic landfills at levels above federal limits. The company has refrained from adopting the ambitious emissions-reduction goal embraced by its main competitor... "It seems very likely that Bill Gates has the power to influence Republic's behavior to make it more climate-friendly, even if that costs the company profits," said Ann Lipton, a legal scholar who studies corporate governance at the University of Colorado, Boulder... Gates didn't respond to repeated requests to discuss his landfill investments, and ProPublica couldn't find any public comments he's made about them. But the bet has proven wildly lucrative. Since November 1999, when he emerged as the owner of 5% of Republic's shares — "It's 'Garbage In' for Gates," the New York Post headline read — the company's stock price has soared thirtyfold. And Gates has personally received $2.6 billion in dividends, a ProPublica analysis of securities filings shows... A rare clue to why Gates made his foray into landfills can be found in an interview he gave to Fortune [in 1999]... To fund his plan to give away virtually his entire fortune, he said he'd given his personal money manager, Michael Larson, a simple remit: Sell Microsoft shares, buy safe, boring assets... After that initial investment, Larson progressively increased Gates' stake in Republic over the years that followed. [On behalf of the Gates Foundation] Larson would also acquire a small chunk of Republic's main competitor, Waste Management. Methane emissions weren't a major focus of climate activism until years later The gas can trap 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide in the near term, and it's responsible for one-third of the global warming we experience today, according to the United Nations Environment Programme. But it also breaks down much more quickly, turning into CO2 and water vapor in about a decade — which means that cutting methane emissions now would reduce that warming within our lifetimes. This is especially urgent, scientists say, as the climate approaches tipping points that could doom rainforests, coral reefs and ice sheets. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: FBI disrupts North Korean FaceStealer campaign behind $5 billion Binance hack
articles.content: The ongoing social-engineering campaign that's reportedly taken $400 million in cryptocurrency from victims and was behind the recent Binance heist now has a name: FaceStealer. The moniker came from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ), who have announced a fight against this crime wave, starting with the seizure of associated cloud infrastructure. According to the DoJ , North Korea is behind these attacks, stealing cryptocurrency to fund its government. The DoJ's press release on the matter is blustery, but the FBI's detailed report contains the important details. The agency's techs seized "cloud-based infrastructure," containing 900 videos of targeted victims. FaceStealer is an advanced form of spear-phishing, complete with AI deepfakes, usage of the victims' contact networks and personal information, and carefully orchestrated preparation — sometimes months in advance. The campaign isn't likely to stop despite the setback, and has reportedly been running for at least 18 months, a timeline that matches up with documented instances of similar intrusion attempts. The largest heist attributed to FaceStealer is the recent Binance hack that saw thieves make out the proverbial door with over $5 billion (most of it thankfully frozen and/or recovered), but far from the only one. The FBI attributes about $400m in stolen cryptocurrency to the campaign, and importantly, also notes that the hackers have repeatedly tried to sneak into open-source software, chiefly Javascript/NPM modules and Rust crates. Despite not being mentioned by name, one example hack is almost certainly the Axios compromise from March 2026. The Node/Javascript library sees about 100 million downloads a week, and temporarily contained a remote-access tool — thankfully for only a few hours. Jason Sayayman, the Axios developer in question, got hooked by an attacker posing as a legitimate company interested in hiring him. The malfeasants replicated the CEO's persona, created a Slack workspace with legitimate-looking channels, then invited him to a Teams meeting with multiple "people." This modus operandi is what the FBI warns about . According to the bureau, FaceStealers start by getting access to a person's communication application(s), then lifting all previous conversations, contact lists, and, most importantly, stealthily recording video of them and/or their contacts. The footage and information will then be used to catch the actual targeted victim, who'll often be sent offers for jobs or investment opportunities. The victim will eventually be invited to a Zoom or Teams meeting that's actually hosted on an attacker-controlled server, with a typo-squatted domain like "uu01webzoom.us" or "teams.livemeet.us". The meeting will often have deepfaked AI participants and/or previous meeting recordings playing, granting the event an air of legitimacy — particularly because conversations leading up to this point will contain real information and context. At some point, though, there will be some sort of "technical problem," and the victim will be prompted to install an "update" or software to fix the problem, which is loaded with malware. From there, the attackers have free rein over the victim's computer and data, and will siphon off browser sessions, CI/CD passwords, and all manners of access credentials to eventually get access to cryptocurrency wallets — or just use this information to find a juicier target, like the poor Binance developer through which Binance's hot wallets were broken into. The FBI says that the above scenario may play out in multiple cycles until the attackers reach their intended target, collecting loads of precious video and information along the way to make the final strike much more convincing.
articles.author: Bruno Ferreira

articles.title: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy
articles.content: Many AI startups are moving fast without a clear direction. (GeekWire Illustration / ChatGPT) The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy. “Hope is not a strategy, and neither is speed.” A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line. Five arguments for speed, and what’s wrong with four of them Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing. Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed. The window is closing . Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one. Competitors are everywhere . AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.” The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box. The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data. Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction. Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed. Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into. Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures. Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not. “Some decisions are consequential and irreversible or nearly irreversible – one-way doors – and these decisions must be made methodically, carefully, slowly, with great deliberation and consultation.” — Jeff Bezos, 2015 letter to shareholders Judgment and defensibility: what…

articles.title: Face ID & telephoto lens are coming to iPhone Duo, eventually
articles.content: While the timetable isn't clear, Apple is reportedly working on adding Face ID to the iPhone Duo . However, the effective engineering deadline for the late 2027 refresh is coming soon, and the feature may not make the cut. Face ID is coming to iPhone Duo, but when is anybody's guess Apple reportedly has two main priorities for the second-generation iPhone Duo. Those are, sensibly, adding Face ID , and adding an Action Button. We've spoken about the Action Button before, and the most likely implementation is a combination with the camera control button. But, the loudest complaints we've heard about the model is about the lack of Face ID. A report on Sunday morning by Mark Gurman claims that prototypes exist with Face ID, with integration into having the VCSEL for the biometrics on the outer display. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: 357 detailed CPU die shots spanning 1971 to 2024 crammed into a new gallery
articles.content: A CPU enthusiast has put together an eye-popping visual database containing crystal-clear, detailed die shots of 357 legendary and some lesser-known processors. At sheets. works/data-viz/cpu-dies, you will find a sortable, searchable, and filterable gallery featuring the outstanding, freely shared die shots from the likes of Pauli Rautakorpi, ZeptoBars, John McMaster, and Fritzchens Fritz . Find one or two of your favorites, and peer into the details to enjoy a nostalgic technological trip down memory lane. That’s what I did. (Image credit: sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies ) The unnamed collator of this gallery might not have contributed any die shots, but has still done an admirable job putting these macrographs and micrographs together in this way. Beneath a brief introduction that credits the skilled photographers who share these images for free, you can glide through the 357-photo collection. By default, the die shot gallery gives you the gallery view, ordered by the oldest silicon first. Those browsing the gallery can instantly switch to a True Scale gallery view, too, which provides some physical sizing context. The next view option for the gallery is a table, where you can see processor maker, year, die dimensions , and photo license at a glance, but it sacrifices visual impact by showing just tiny thumbnails. sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies sheets.works/data-viz/cpu-dies Navigating the gallery is also quick and intuitive thanks to a built-in search function. Using this, it was easy to display only 486 CPU s, for example. For your information, there are 17 486 CPU variants in this gallery with samples produced by AMD, Cyrix , IBM, TI, UMC, VLSI, and Intel of course. You can click any of the thumbnails to jump to a larger view with notes of the design, as well as photographer details/credits. Though that click zooms in the image considerably, I found that a right-click – open image in new tab - was needed to enjoy the die shot’s full visual splendor. It would be great to see the database/gallery maintained with the latest shareable die shots from the various contributors. Also, it could be improved by fully populating details such as the die area, which is not always present. Some more searchable and sortable fields, such as transistor count, might also make this resource more satisfying. For my personal nostalgia, I enjoyed seeing CPUs like the Motorola 68000 and the AMD Athlon XP up close. Surprisingly, some eras, including the Intel Ivy Bridge and Haswell generations, seemed underrepresented, though.
articles.author: Mark Tyson

articles.title: The new Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it
articles.content: The new Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well. However, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box. more…

articles.title: Microsoft 365 outage leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
articles.content: Fifteen guests at a hotel in Germany suffered from chlorine gas poisoning because of the recent Microsoft cloud services outage. The establishment had a “maintenance safety system” for its sauna area that relied on sending emails to warn the operators if the chlorine level in the area was too high. Unfortunately, the service disruption meant that the system's messages could not be sent, leading to increased levels that precipitated human injuries, writes Notebookcheck . German emergency services had to deploy 40 first responders to the site, with local media reporting that four victims were taken to the hospital for treatment, with one remaining for further observation. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible The tech giant experienced a global outage affecting Outlook and other services from November 12 to 14, which led some Japanese workers to dust off their fax machines to keep their business running. Although this Microsoft outage wasn’t as large as the CrowdStrike fiasco in 2024 , which led to a massive service disruption to a good number of corporate computer systems and sent shockwaves across the world, this incident has caused injuries and could’ve even led to something more catastrophic if the issue wasn’t caught earlier. This is one of the issues that institutions must consider when using online services or the Internet of Things to automate systems, especially those that are crucial for safety. Architects of such systems should always have a physical or analog backup that will continue operating even if everything goes offline. More importantly, their people should know that they exist and be familiar with how they work. Alternatively, businesses can host their own servers, build their own automations, and run everything locally, although this would require a bit more involvement in building and programming the entire system. And there could be local infrastructure impacting issues like power cuts, still. Aside from that, the Microsoft outage also highlights the corporate world’s increasing reliance on a few big tech companies. While tech giants like Microsoft, Google, and AWS have the advantage of economies of scale, allowing them to offer their services reliably and more affordably compared to smaller rivals or an in-house deployment, it also means that if they go down, they affect millions of businesses that rely on them and cause economic activity to grind to a halt.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Rust Leaves Top 10 in TIOBE Index, Making Room for Go
articles.content: "In November's edition of the TIOBE Index, Rust has dropped out of Top 10," writes I-Programmer, noting that Rust ceded the #10 position to Go. "At the same time, another Google-originated language, Dart, has entered the top 20 ousting Julia after only one month." TIOBE explains Dart's popularity is mainly being driven by Flutter, Google's framework for building cross-platform mobile applications. In fact, Flutter has become one of the major technologies for cross-platform mobile app development. The Dart language itself is not particularly unique, although it incorporates many modern programming language features. Its success is largely driven by the strength of the Flutter ecosystem and the convenience of developing applications for multiple platforms using a single codebase... [In November's ranking] Visual Basic has also lost two places, making room for R and SQL in the Top 10. Further down the ranking, Assembly has re-entered the Top 20. So TIOBE ranks the top 10 languages in November as Python, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, and Go. But I-Programmer points out that "At the top of the table, Java is back in the top 3, after over three years in 4th position," pushing C++ down to #4. Are some changes more significant than others? If you think of the ratings as shares of a pie divided into 100 pieces, there is one huge slice — Python, accounting for a over a fifth of the pie, then comes C with a slice slightly less than half of Python's. Java and C++ then have smaller slices... and C#'s share is around half of their average size. Over half the pie has now been shared between just five languages... — Next 5 (#6-10): 10.17% (JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, Go) — Next 10 (#11-20): 11.12% (Rust, PHP, Fortran, Scratch, Perl, MATLAB, Assembly, Swift, Delphi, Dart) — Next 30 (#21-50): 12.81% — Final 50 (#51-100): 12.93% [So in this month's chart...] Java has overtaken C++, but as you can see from this month's Top 10 chart they are in lock step and the difference between them is insignificant. More obvious is that Python is way ahead of all the competition and that C has an edge over Java and C++. For more discussion of this see TIOBE — Two To Rule Them All in which Mike James argued that this: confirms the standard model of programming - code is written in Python and C and everything else is just noise. Back in July we reported Rust Enters TIOBE Top 10. After four months in #10 Rust is now back at #11, which is still three places above its position, 14, a year ago. Given the way these rankings operate it only takes a very small month-on-month change for a language to lose its position and even, as has happened here it can gain in terms of its percentage ranking while still moving down. So Rust with 1.63% in November is now in #11 when it had been in #10 with 1.44%. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
